blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
At 2:47 a.m. São Paulo time on the night Crescent went live in three regions, a single customer named Adaeze Okafor — a Nigerian software engineer living in São Paulo's Vila Madalena — bought a 6-real data bundle from her phone. She paid once. The phone showed one receipt. Her bank statement showed two charges.

Olamide woke up to the page at 3:04. By 3:30 she was reading the trace. Two coordinator nodes, one in Crescent's EU-West region (a Frankfurt datacenter) and one in the South America gateway that fronts Crescent's US-East region (the gateway sits in São Paulo, routing into US-East for the operational data plane), had each completed the payment. Each had logged a clean commit. Each believed it was the only coordinator handling that transaction. The customer's phone, sitting on a flaky 3G connection, had retried the request once when the first response was slow, and the retry had landed on the São Paulo gateway while the original was still finishing through Frankfurt. (Chapters 13 and 28 develop Crescent's three-region architecture — US-East, EU-West, US-West — in full; this chapter uses the city names because that is how the post-mortem first named them, before the team reframed the discussion in region terms.)

The bug was not in any single piece of code. The bank's ledger code was correct. The retry logic was correct. The payment gateway's idempotency check was correct, for the model of the world it had. The bug was in what each component believed about the others. Each component believed something that was not, in fact, true.

This book is about systems that believe things that are not true. It is about the discipline of building software that knows when to doubt itself.


### 1.1 The Three Lies

When you write a program that runs on one machine, the machine is honest with you. The clock advances. Variables hold the values you set. When a function returns, it has returned. When you call it twice, you have called it twice.

When you write a program that runs on more than one machine, none of this is true.

The two coordinators in the Crescent incident lied to each other about three things, and the three things are not arbitrary. They are the three lies that every distributed system tells, and they recur in every failure post-mortem you will ever read in this field.


#### The First Lie: Time

The Frankfurt coordinator stamped the transaction with its local clock at 02:47:18.412 UTC. The São Paulo coordinator stamped its version at 02:47:18.407 UTC. By the clocks, the São Paulo transaction happened first. By the customer's experience, the Frankfurt one came first. By the wire arrival times at the bank, neither was first because the messages arrived in a different order at different downstream services.

The clocks were not broken. They were running NTP. They were within 5 ms of each other, which is good. The lie was not in the clocks. The lie was in the assumption that 5 ms is enough resolution to order events that happen 5 ms apart on different machines.

Chapter 3 is about this lie in depth. The short version: there is no global "now" in a distributed system. Anyone who writes `if event_a.timestamp < event_b.timestamp` to decide which event happened first is reasoning about a fiction.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### The Second Lie: Identity

The Frankfurt coordinator believed it was the only coordinator handling Adaeze's transaction. The São Paulo coordinator believed the same. Both were correct from inside their own view of the world. Both were wrong from outside.

This is the lie of identity: each node sees itself as a singular actor with a coherent view of the system. From inside the node, this is a useful fiction. From outside, the node is one of many, and the others may believe contradictory things about what it is, what role it is playing, and whether it is even alive.

The lie of identity is what makes distributed locks hard. It is what makes leader election hard. It is what makes consensus hard. Every protocol in Chapters 7 through 10 exists to reduce, not eliminate, the gap between what one node believes about itself and what the rest of the system believes about it.


#### The Third Lie: Failure

The Frankfurt coordinator never observed a failure. It sent its message to the bank. The bank acknowledged. The transaction completed. From Frankfurt's logs, the system was healthy throughout.

São Paulo also never observed a failure. From its logs, the system was equally healthy.

But the system as a whole had failed. The customer was double-charged. The bank's ledger had two debits where there should have been one.

This is the third lie, and it is the deepest. In a single-machine program, failure is loud. The process crashes. The disk fills. The exception propagates up the stack. You see it. In a distributed system, failure is almost always partial. Half of a transaction succeeds. A message is delivered to two of three replicas. A node is responsive to its own monitoring but dropping every third request from elsewhere.

The single-machine model treats failure as an exception. The distributed model treats partial failure as the default mode. If you write distributed code that handles only the happy path and treats failure as an unusual exception, you are writing code that will, eventually, double-charge Adaeze.


### 1.2 What Makes Distributed Reasoning Different

Most engineers learn to program in a world that lies pleasantly. The clock is accurate. Function calls return. Memory holds what you put there. State changes happen one at a time, in a known order, on a known machine.

When you step into distributed systems, every one of those guarantees weakens or disappears. The hard part is not learning new APIs. The hard part is unlearning the intuitions you built in the single-machine world.


#### Common Misconception

Many engineers, on first encountering distributed systems, believe the difficulty is about performance. They think: "Distributed systems are about making things fast by spreading them across many machines."

This is the wrong frame. Performance is sometimes a benefit. The first reason most large systems are distributed is that they have no choice. The data does not fit on one machine. The users are not in one geography. The load exceeds one server's capacity. The system needs to survive when individual machines fail.

The hard part is not the speed. The hard part is that splitting work across machines introduces the three lies, and now your code has to be correct in their presence. A "fast" distributed system that double-charges customers is not a fast system. It is a broken one.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### Why partial failure is the right mental default

In a single-machine program, the probability that the program experiences a hardware failure during a one-second window is roughly the probability of one machine failing, which is small. Maybe one in a billion seconds, depending on the hardware.

In a system of 10,000 machines, the probability that _some_ machine experiences a failure during any given second approaches one. At Google scale, the question is not "did anything fail?" but "what failed in the last hour and was the damage contained?"

This is the operational reality that distributed-systems engineers internalize. It is not pessimism. It is arithmetic. If you build for the case where nothing ever fails, you are building for a world that does not exist at scale.


### 1.3 The Working Engineer's Question

This book teaches one mental move. When you look at any distributed system, you ask three questions:

  1. **What is this system lying about time?** Does it assume `time.Now()` orders events? Does it assume timestamps are comparable across machines? Does it assume sessions begin and end at well-defined moments?
  2. **What is this system lying about identity?** Does it assume one node is "the leader" without a protocol to prove it? Does it assume locks are unique without fencing tokens? Does it assume the node it is talking to is the node it thinks it is talking to?
  3. **What is this system lying about failure?** Does it have a happy path and an error path, with the error path being the unusual case? Does it treat retries as idempotent without proof? Does it have any code path that assumes "this won't happen"?

If you can answer these three questions about any system, you can reason about its failure modes. If you cannot answer them, you do not yet understand the system, no matter how well you understand its API.

The four protagonists you will meet in this book all run this loop, on different systems, in different domains. Olamide runs it on the multi-region payment platform you just met. Yuki Watanabe runs it on collaborative document editors at Glide. Tobias Schwartz runs it on the LLM inference cluster at Continuum Inference. Anya Reddy runs it inside the database engine at Stratus DB. The systems are different. The mental move is the same.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
### 1.4 What This Book Is Not

This book is not a survey of every paper in the field. It is not a reimplementation tutorial for any single database. It is not a Kubernetes book and it is not a blockchain book. The reference for the foundational material is Kleppmann's _Designing Data-Intensive Applications_ ; if you have not read it, read it after this one, or in parallel.

What this book is: an operating manual for the working distributed-systems engineer in 2026. The systems named by name (Spanner, CockroachDB, FoundationDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, Aurora DSQL, TigerBeetle, vLLM, SGLang, NVIDIA NIM) are the systems you will actually deploy or evaluate this year. The protocols named (Raft, Paxos, HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Percolator, Calvin) are the ones currently running in production. The failure modes named (metastable, gray, cascading) are the ones currently writing post-mortems.

The book is also, deliberately, a book about a particular thing that has changed in the last two years: AI-assisted code generation. Distributed code is the worst category for LLM generation, and Chapter 27 returns to this in full. For now, hold the observation: if there is one part of a codebase where you should not trust generated output without verification, it is the part that crosses a network boundary.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### What this book deliberately does not cover

Several adjacent topics are out of scope. Each is real and worth study; each has its own canonical references; each would distort this book's focus if included.

* **Storage-engine internals at depth** : LSM-tree compaction tuning, Bloom-filter sizing, B+ tree write-amplification optimization, page-cache behavior, fsync ordering. We touch these where they affect distributed-systems reasoning (Chapter 12) but do not develop the single-node depth. References: Kleppmann's _DDIA_ chapters 3-4 (foundations); the RocksDB tuning guide (operational depth); Pavlo & Aslett's CMU 15-721 lectures (academic depth).
* **Network observability at depth** : eBPF-based service-mesh observability, OpenTelemetry collector pipeline tuning, log/metric/trace storage backends. Chapter 20 covers what tracing tells you about distributed-systems behavior; the pipeline machinery is the topic of Series IV Vol 3 (Observability). References: Sridharan _Distributed Systems Observability_ (O'Reilly, 2018); the Cilium / Hubble docs for eBPF; the OpenTelemetry Collector documentation.
* **Federated learning and privacy-preserving computation** : differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, homomorphic encryption applied to distributed ML. These are distributed-systems-adjacent in 2026 but constitute their own discipline. References: Mohri's _Federated Learning_ (2023); Kairouz et al. "Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning" (2021); the OpenMined community materials; Dwork & Roth _The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy_ (2014).
* **Quantum-network protocols** : quantum key distribution, entanglement-distribution protocols, quantum-classical hybrid consensus. As of 2026, these are research topics, not production reality; the engineer reading this book should not need them in the next 5 years. References: Wehner, Elkouss, Hanson "Quantum internet: A vision for the road ahead" (_Science_ , 2018); the QED-C industry consortium reports.
* **Single-system administration** : Linux kernel tuning, container runtime internals, hypervisor selection. These are the substrate on which distributed systems run but the substrate's specifics are out of scope. References: Bovet & Cesati _Understanding the Linux Kernel_ (3rd ed.); Love _Linux System Programming_ ; Brendan Gregg's _Systems Performance_ (2nd ed., 2020).
* **Application-layer protocols at depth** : REST API design (covered in _Software at Scale_ Series IV Vol 1, _APIs_), gRPC schema evolution, OpenAPI tooling. Chapter 19 mentions service discovery; the protocols themselves are out of scope. References: Newman _Building Microservices_ (2nd ed., 2021); Richardson & Ruby _RESTful Web Services_ ; the official gRPC and OpenAPI specifications.

The discipline of _staying scoped_ is itself a distributed-systems skill. A book that tries to cover everything is unhelpful in production; a book scoped to the questions the working engineer must ask is useful. This book is scoped to the latter.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
### 1.5 Reading the Book

The book proceeds in nine parts. Part I (Chapters 1 through 3) sets up the mental model. Part II (Chapters 4 through 6) introduces broadcast and replication primitives. Part III (Chapters 7 through 10) is consensus. Part IV (Chapters 11 through 14) is distributed databases. Part V (Chapters 15 through 17) is eventual consistency and CRDTs. Part VI (Chapters 18 through 19) is coordination. Part VII (Chapters 20 through 23) is operating distributed systems at scale. Part VIII (Chapters 24 through 26) is distributed LLM inference, which is a 2026 sub-discipline. Part IX (Chapters 27 through 28) synthesizes the book. Chapter 29 is a Postscript on the 2027-2030 horizon, sitting outside the nine-part structure but recommended at the end of any reading path; it identifies which named systems and primitives will likely evolve and which aspects of the mental model are durable.

Each chapter is meant to support roughly four to five working sessions with the Socratopia companion. You read it once for the structure. The companion reads it with you, asks questions, watches you work through examples, and probes the misconceptions documented in each chapter. The questions at the end of each chapter are not summative tests. They are starting points for those sessions.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### How to use this book based on your role

Different readers will get the most value from different paths through the material.

* **Complete newcomer to distributed systems** : read in order, Chapter 1 → Chapter 29 (Chapter 29 is the forward-look Postscript). Plan 4-5 Socratopia sessions per chapter; expect 12-16 weeks for the full arc. Do the Concept Check exercises after each chapter; the Application Problems after Part III; the Think Deeper questions at end of each Part.

* **Backend / infrastructure engineer with DDIA background** : skim Chapters 2 (CAP/PACELC restatement) and 5 (replication) which overlap with DDIA. Read Chapters 3 (HLC adds to DDIA's clocks chapter), 6 (multi-region not deeply in DDIA), 9 (Raft developed beyond DDIA), 10 (BFT, beyond DDIA), 11 (the diagnostic method), 13 (modern transactions including saga §13.6.5), 14 (NewSQL landscape), 24-26 (LLM inference, not in DDIA), 27-29 (synthesis + 2027-2030 forward look). Plan 2-3 sessions per chapter; ~6 weeks.

* **SRE / operations engineer** : priority order is Part VII (Ch.20-23), then Ch.27 §27.10 (AI-assisted review of distributed code), then Ch.28 (synthesis showing how it all fits). Then loop back to Ch.11 (diagnostic method for any new system you're handed) and Ch.6 (latency budgets). Plan ~4 weeks for the SRE-focused subset.

* **AI infrastructure engineer (vLLM / SGLang / inference platforms)** : start with Part VIII (Ch.24-26), then Ch.27 (LLM-generated code review), then loop back to Chapters 1-3 (mental model) + 9 (Raft, since inference clusters use it for coordination state). The diagnostic method (Ch.11) generalizes from databases to inference systems. Plan ~3 weeks for the inference-focused subset.

* **Distributed-systems instructor** : use Ch.1 §1.1-1.3 (three lies) as the framing for the entire course. Use the cold-hook chapters of Thread C (Ch.2, 3, 4, 18, 21, 22) as discussion-leading examples. Use Ch.27 §27.10 (AI-assisted reviewing) as a contemporary capstone discussion. The 12 binding workflows (Ch.28 §28.7) can each anchor a week of a semester course.

* **Reference user (already know the field, looking up specifics)** : Appendix A (reading list by chapter) is your index; Appendix B (5-database CAP reference), Appendix C (glossary), Appendix D (six lies card), Appendix E (case studies), Appendix F (decision tree by workload) are designed for one-page lookups. Ch.11 (diagnostic method) and Ch.14 (NewSQL matrix) are the most often re-consulted body chapters.

* **PR reviewer auditing AI-generated distributed code** : read Ch.27 first (the six lies and the checklist), then Ch.18 (fencing tokens), Ch.21 (retry budgets and circuit breakers), Ch.13 §13.6.5 (saga). Keep Appendix D (six lies card) at hand during reviews. Read Ch.27 §27.10 (three-layer architecture, rubber-stamping anti-pattern) before establishing team review policy.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### A note on the exercises

The exercises at the end of each chapter are structured for the Socratopia companion to guide you through, not as summative tests. The Concept Check items test recall + understanding; the Application Problems exercise transfer (apply the concept to a new scenario); the Think Deeper items are open-ended discussions where the companion can take both sides. Hints are folded into `<details>` tags; consult them only after honestly trying the question first.

The 12 binding workflows (catalogued at Ch.28 §28.7) are not numbered exercises but recurring patterns to internalize. Each appears in one designated chapter as a full walkthrough; ability to execute each one independently is the operational test of having absorbed the corresponding chapter.

Now back to Adaeze. By 6:00 a.m. Olamide had a fix. By 9:00 a.m. she had a post-mortem. The fix involved fencing tokens (Chapter 18), Hybrid Logical Clocks (Chapter 3), and a Raft-backed commit log for the coordinator state (Chapter 9). The post-mortem named all three lies the system had been telling. The bank refunded Adaeze. Crescent published the post-mortem internally and ran a game day (Chapter 23) the following week to verify that the fix held under simulated partition.

The system Crescent runs now is the system Olamide, Anya, Yuki, and Tobias finally ship together in Chapter 28. The path between Chapter 1 and Chapter 28 is the book proper; Chapter 29 then looks forward to how that system will evolve through 2027-2030, separating the durable parts of the mental model from the named-system details that will age.


### 1.6 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** In your own words, state the three lies that every distributed system tells. For each, give one concrete example of code that assumes the lie is the truth.

Hint

The lies are about time, identity, and failure. Look for code patterns: comparing timestamps across machines, assuming a lock holder is unique, assuming an RPC either succeeds or visibly fails.

**Answer:** The three lies are time, identity, and failure.

_Time_ : code that assumes machine clocks are comparable. Example: `if user_event.timestamp < server_event.timestamp: process_in_order()`. This compares a client-machine timestamp to a server-machine timestamp without accounting for clock skew. NTP keeps machines within milliseconds of each other on a good day; on a bad day or behind a firewall, they can drift by seconds or more. The comparison can produce the wrong ordering and the code will silently process events in the wrong order.

_Identity_ : code that assumes one process is uniquely "the leader" without a protocol that proves it. Example: `if redis.set("leader_lock", node_id, nx=True, ex=30): become_leader()`. This is the Redlock pattern (Chapter 18). It assumes that holding the lock for 30 seconds means no other node holds it. Under network partition or GC pause, two nodes can each believe they hold the lock, and both will act as leader.

_Failure_ : code that has a happy path and treats failure as exceptional. Example: `result = remote_service.call(); update_local_state(result)`. The `remote_service.call()` can succeed remotely while the response is lost, can fail visibly, can hang for an unknown duration, or can be delivered twice if the network or transport layer retries it. Treating the success case as the default and the visible failure as the exception ignores the largest category: partial visibility.

**Q2.** The Crescent incident involved a single retry on a flaky mobile connection. Walk through what would have prevented it for each lie independently. Why was no single fix sufficient?

Hint

Each lie required a different discipline. Idempotency tokens address one. Coordinator uniqueness via fencing tokens addresses another. Clock-skew-bounded timestamps address the third.

**Answer:** For the lie of failure, an idempotency token on the request would have caused the second coordinator's retry to be recognized as "I have already processed this transaction ID" and refused — the second commit becomes a no-op rather than a duplicate charge. The bank's idempotency check was supposed to do this but operated on a window that was too short; the second request arrived just outside the window.

For the lie of time, using Hybrid Logical Clock timestamps (Chapter 3) rather than wall-clock timestamps would have given both coordinators the same comparable ordering. Either coordinator would have seen the other's commit had occurred first in HLC time, even if both completed in the same 5 ms window of NTP-clock time.

For the lie of identity, a fencing token (Chapter 18) on the coordinator role would have caused the bank to reject the second commit because the second coordinator's token would have been lower than the first's. Even if both believed they were the active coordinator, the bank would have known which one to trust based on the monotonic token order.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
No single fix was sufficient because the incident exploited all three lies at once. The retry caused two coordinators to be active (identity). Their clocks could not agree on order (time). Neither could detect the other's existence in time to abort (failure). Defense in depth is the rule: name the three lies separately and harden against each.

**Q3.** A junior engineer says: "We don't need to worry about clock skew because all our servers run NTP and stay within 10 ms of each other." Identify three failure modes this reasoning does not cover.

Hint

Consider what happens during NTP outages, during virtual-machine pauses, and at the boundaries of the 10 ms window.

**Answer:** First, the 10 ms window itself is enough room for the Crescent-style failure. If two coordinators commit within 10 ms of each other, the timestamps cannot reliably order them. Many distributed bugs live in windows smaller than the clock-skew bound.

Second, NTP can fail silently. If the NTP server becomes unreachable, the local clock drifts at the hardware's rate, which on a typical server is up to seconds per day. A node that lost NTP last Tuesday and has been drifting since can be many seconds off and still respond to requests as if healthy.

Third, virtual-machine pauses make a single machine's clock jump. A VM that is paused for 30 seconds by the hypervisor (snapshot, live migration, garbage-collection STW pause on certain runtimes) experiences its wall clock jump by 30 seconds when it resumes. From the outside, the node appears to have time-traveled forward. Inside the node, any code reasoning about durations between two clock reads on either side of the pause produces nonsense.

**Q4.** Define partial failure in your own words and contrast it with the single-machine notion of failure. Give one example of each.

Hint

On a single machine, failure is loud (process crash, exception). In a distributed system, the canonical failure is "I asked X to do something and I don't know what happened."

**Answer:** A single-machine failure is loud and complete. The process crashes; the disk hits ENOSPC; the function throws. You see it because the failure is local and observable. Example: `open("/tmp/file", "w")` returns an error because the disk is full. The program receives the error, can decide what to do, and is in a known state.

A partial failure is incomplete and silent. Part of the work happened; part did not; the boundary between the two is unobservable from at least one participant. Example: client sends an HTTP POST to a service. The service receives the request, performs the side effect (charging the card), and crashes before sending the response. The client times out, retries, and the service (now restarted) receives the duplicate. From the client's perspective, the first request failed. From the service's records, both requests succeeded. There is no single observer who has the truth; the truth is split across nodes, and the system must be designed so that this split does not corrupt user-visible state.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** You are reading a stack trace for a payment service that has double-charged a customer. The trace shows two POST `/charge` requests, both with the same idempotency key, arriving 47 ms apart at two different replicas of the payment service. Both succeeded. Walk through the three lies and identify which one the system failed to defend against.

Hint

The idempotency key is the system's defense against the lie of failure (it makes retries safe). What went wrong despite that defense?

**Answer:** The system attempted to defend against the lie of failure with the idempotency key. The defense relies on a single source of truth that can recognize "I have already processed this key." If the two replicas share a strongly consistent store of seen idempotency keys (for example, a Spanner or CockroachDB table with a unique constraint), the second request fails the constraint and the duplicate charge is prevented.

If both replicas instead consulted a local cache or a per-region store that had not yet replicated the first request's entry, neither saw the other's prior commit. The system failed the lie of identity at the storage layer: the system believed there was one "idempotency record store," but in reality there were two views of it, briefly inconsistent.

The fix is to make the idempotency check go through a strongly consistent path (the Percolator-style transaction of Chapter 13, or a Raft-replicated commit log of Chapter 9). The cheaper-but-wrong fix is to make the idempotency window longer, which only buys time before the next near-simultaneous retry hits the same gap.

**Q2.** You join a team that is building a leader-election protocol for a configuration service. A senior engineer says: "We're using Redis with `SET NX EX 30` to elect the leader. The leader refreshes the key every 10 seconds. If a leader dies, the key expires and someone else takes over." Identify three failure modes the design does not handle. Reference Chapter 18 if you need to.

Hint

The pattern is Redlock. The Jepsen / Kleppmann debate identified at least three failure modes. Think about GC pauses, network partitions to Redis, and what happens when an old leader wakes up.

**Answer:** First, a long GC pause on the leader (or a VM pause, or any other stop-the-world event) can cause the leader to fail to refresh the lock in time. The lock expires; a new leader takes over; then the original leader wakes up and continues to act as leader, believing it still holds the lock because no exception ever fired. Two leaders are now active.

Second, a network partition between the leader and Redis can cause the same situation from a different cause. The leader cannot refresh, the lock expires, a new leader is elected via a different network path, and when the partition heals, the original leader is still acting as leader from its perspective.

Third, even if the lock genuinely is uniquely held, there is no fencing token. An action issued by an old leader (which began before its lock expired but has not yet been delivered to the downstream system) arrives at the downstream after a new leader has issued its own action. The downstream system has no way to distinguish "issued by current leader" from "issued by stale leader," so it processes both.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
The fix is a fencing token, covered in Chapter 18: each lock acquisition increases a monotonic counter, and every downstream action carries the token. The downstream rejects any action whose token is lower than the highest token it has seen. This works even when two nodes briefly believe they hold the lock, because only the one with the higher token can persuade the downstream to act.

**Q3.** A microservice architecture has 14 services and a single request typically touches 5 to 8 of them. One of the services is intermittently slow (it works, but returns in 5 to 8 seconds instead of the expected 50 ms). What kinds of distributed failures might this cause in the rest of the system? Identify at least three.

Hint

Slow services cause back-pressure, timeouts, and retry storms (Chapter 21). They also pass health checks while being effectively broken (Chapter 22 — gray failure).

**Answer:** First, callers of the slow service time out, retry, and contribute to a retry storm. If each upstream service retries three times with a 5-second timeout, and each retry queues a fresh request that the slow service must also serve, the queue depth at the slow service grows unboundedly until the entire upstream collapses. This is the cascading-failure dynamic of Chapter 21.

Second, the slow service may pass its own health check while being effectively unusable. Its health check returns 200 OK in milliseconds because the health check is a cheap endpoint that does not touch the slow code path. Load balancers continue to route requests to it. This is the gray-failure pattern of Chapter 22, and it is precisely the worst case for monitoring because the system reports "healthy" while the user reports "broken."

Third, downstream services that depend on the slow service via synchronous calls inherit its latency. A request that should complete in 200 ms ends up taking 8 seconds because one hop in the chain is slow. Resource pools (database connections, thread pools, request slots) fill up holding requests waiting on the slow service. Eventually the downstream service exhausts its pool and starts rejecting requests that have nothing to do with the slow dependency. This is the cross-service contagion of cascading failure.

**Q4.** Pick any distributed system you have used recently (a database, a cache, a queue, a key-value store). Without reading documentation, write down what you believe the system promises about time, identity, and failure. Then look at its documentation and identify one assumption you held that was wrong.

Hint

This is the exercise the rest of the book will train you on. The point is to notice the gap between what you assume and what the system promises.

**Answer:** The discipline here is more important than any specific answer. A worked example: a Postgres reader who assumes "if I do `SELECT now()` and then `INSERT INTO log (created_at) VALUES (now())`, the inserted row's timestamp matches the SELECT" will be surprised to learn that `now()` in Postgres returns the _transaction start time_ , not the wall-clock time at the moment of the call. Two statements in the same transaction see the same `now()`. This is documented but contrary to the naive single-machine intuition.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src: In general, the lies you held that were wrong tend to cluster around: (a) what "now" means in this system, (b) whether the system guarantees uniqueness of something you assumed was unique, (c) what happens when the system or your client crashes mid-operation. The rest of the book builds the vocabulary for asking these questions precisely.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Many engineers, after their first serious distributed-systems failure, decide "I'll keep everything on one machine for as long as possible." Defend or critique this position. Under what conditions is it correct, and under what conditions is it a trap?

**Discussion:** The position has real merit. A correctly engineered single-machine system handles many problems with vastly less complexity than any distributed equivalent. Postgres on one box, replicated to a hot standby, can serve enormous load with strong consistency. The decision to go distributed has real costs and should not be taken lightly.

The position becomes a trap when the requirements quietly outgrow it. The system that started as "one Postgres" needs read replicas (now you have replication lag and read-your-writes failures). It needs cross-region for latency or disaster recovery (now you have multi-region replication). It needs partition tolerance for an SLA (now you are in CAP territory whether you named it or not). At each step, distributed concerns crept in without the team formally adopting distributed disciplines, and the resulting system has all the failure modes of a distributed system with none of the rigor.

The honest answer is: stay single-machine as long as the requirements truly are single-machine. The moment you add a second machine for any reason, name the distributed disciplines that now apply (time, identity, failure) and verify that you are handling them.

A second consideration: in 2026, "single machine" is itself a fiction at the scale of the largest workloads. A modern database deployment may be one logical instance backed by a distributed storage layer (Aurora, Neon), so even when the application thinks it is talking to one Postgres, the storage is already distributed and inherits all three lies.

**Q2.** The Crescent post-mortem named three lies and required fixes for all three. In your experience or reading, find one production incident where the responders fixed only the most visible failure and missed a deeper lie. What is the cost pattern when this happens?

**Discussion:** The pattern repeats: a visible bug gets fixed, the same class of bug appears six months later under slightly different conditions, and only on the second or third occurrence does someone identify the deeper lie. The cost is the cumulative incident response, the customer impact, and the engineering time spent on each fix in succession.

Examples to look for in your reading: post-mortems that fix a retry storm by tuning timeouts (without addressing the underlying lack of retry budgets or circuit breakers); incidents that fix a leader-election bug by increasing the lock TTL (without introducing fencing tokens); duplicate-charge incidents that widen the idempotency window (without making the idempotency check strongly consistent).

A useful frame: each of these "tuning" fixes makes the same failure rarer without changing its category. The honest fix changes the category. If you find yourself reading a post-mortem that ends with "we increased the timeout," it is worth asking: what would the post-mortem have said if the timeout were already infinite?

blocks.en_title: Chapter 1: Distributed Systems Lie to Themselves
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

Distributed systems lie to themselves about three things. They lie about time: the clocks are not synchronized at the resolution your code assumes. They lie about identity: each node sees itself as uniquely playing its role, while the rest of the system may disagree. They lie about failure: partial failure is the default mode, not the exception, and the gap between "what happened on this node" and "what the system as a whole experienced" is where the bugs live.

The Crescent incident exploited all three lies in a single retry. The fix involved fencing tokens (Chapter 18), Hybrid Logical Clocks (Chapter 3), and a Raft-backed commit log (Chapter 9). No single fix would have closed the gap.

The mental move this book trains is simple: when you encounter any distributed system, ask the three questions. What is it lying about time? About identity? About failure? If you can answer, you can reason about failure modes. If you cannot, the system is opaque to you regardless of how well you know its API.

The chapter ahead (Chapter 2) makes these lies quantitative. You will meet Deutsch's Eight Fallacies (which name them as engineering assumptions), CAP (which quantifies the trade-off between consistency and availability under partition), and PACELC (which extends CAP to the no-partition case). Then Chapter 3 takes the first lie, time, and develops the protocols (Lamport clocks, vector clocks, HLC, TrueTime) that let you reason about ordering without lying.

The book will keep returning to Adaeze. The system that double-charged her in the second-to-last paragraph of this chapter is the system the four protagonists ship together in Chapter 28. Everything in between is the path; Chapter 29 closes the book by separating what will keep evolving from what will hold.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
An LLM, asked to write a distributed inventory service, produces 200 lines of clean-looking Python. The prose around the code says: "We use a strongly consistent database (CockroachDB) to ensure that no item is ever oversold. This gives us a CP system per CAP." The code is plausible. The comment is plausible. Both are wrong, and the gap between "plausible" and "correct" is the subject of this chapter. (As with every LLM cold-hook code reference in this book, the bug is structural — a slogan-level CAP claim that hides the per-operation question — not syntactic.)

The model picked CP because the prose around CockroachDB on the internet says CockroachDB is CP. The model did not name that CockroachDB's default isolation level is serializable, that its commit latency depends on whether the data is in a single region or multi-region, that "consistent" in CAP means linearizable (a much stronger property than "transactional"), or that the latency the application sees has more to do with PACELC (the C-and-L trade-off when there is no partition) than with C-or-A under partition.

This chapter teaches you the difference between knowing the labels (CP, AP, eventual, strong) and reasoning about what they actually cost. We start with Deutsch's Eight Fallacies, because they name the assumptions that every wrong distributed-systems intuition rests on. Then CAP, stated precisely (not as slogan), then PACELC, which extends CAP to the case CAP ignores.


### 2.1 Deutsch's Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing

In the early 1990s, Peter Deutsch at Sun Microsystems wrote down a list of false assumptions that engineers new to distributed computing tend to make. James Gosling later added an eighth. The list has aged well because the fallacies are not about specific technologies; they are about the gap between single-machine intuition and distributed reality.

The eight fallacies:

  1. **The network is reliable.**
  2. **Latency is zero.**
  3. **Bandwidth is infinite.**
  4. **The network is secure.**
  5. **Topology doesn't change.**
  6. **There is one administrator.**
  7. **Transport cost is zero.**
  8. **The network is homogeneous.**

Each fallacy maps to a category of bug. We will work through them quickly because the rest of the book will return to most of them in depth.


#### The network is reliable

Packets are dropped. TCP retransmits, but TCP itself can give up after enough retries and report the connection broken. HTTP layered on TCP inherits this. When your code calls `http.post(url)` and gets back a timeout, you do not know whether the request was processed; you know only that you did not receive the response.

This single fallacy is the root of the third lie of Chapter 1 (the lie of failure). The code patterns that assume "RPC has TCP-like semantics" all start here. We will come back to the network in Chapter 21, where its unreliability causes cascading failures, and in Chapter 18, where it ruins naive distributed locks.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### Latency is zero

A function call within a process is on the order of nanoseconds. A function call to a different machine in the same datacenter is on the order of 100 microseconds when nothing is wrong. A call across an ocean is on the order of 100 milliseconds, and is bounded by the speed of light, which is not negotiable.

The numbers matter because they invert the cost of operations. A single-machine algorithm that does a million memory accesses runs in milliseconds. The same algorithm distributed across two machines, doing a million RPCs, runs in minutes. The algorithm is not "the same." Going distributed forces you to redesign the access pattern.


#### Bandwidth is infinite

The hot-pixel data of an autonomous vehicle is 4 GB/s per camera, eight cameras per vehicle, hundreds of thousands of vehicles. The latency budget for 5G uplink is bounded. Many "real-time" pipelines fail not because the data is hard to compute but because there is no path with enough bandwidth to move it where it needs to go.


#### The network is secure

Every packet is open by default. Encryption is opt-in. TLS is encryption between two endpoints; it does not authenticate the endpoints unless certificate validation is correct, and it does not protect against an authenticated endpoint that has been compromised. The fact that your traffic is "over HTTPS" tells you almost nothing about whether the system is secure.


#### Topology doesn't change

The list of machines in your cluster changes. Containers come and go. Auto-scaling brings up nodes. DNS records update. The IP address that resolved to your service yesterday may resolve to a different service tomorrow. Code that hard-codes IPs, hard-codes hostnames without retry-on-DNS-failure, or assumes the membership of a cluster is stable will break.


#### There is one administrator

Different parts of the system are operated by different teams, possibly different companies. The team running your service does not control the database team's deploys, the network team's firewall changes, or the cloud provider's maintenance windows. A change in any one of these can break your system without warning, and the people who made the change may not know your system exists.


#### Transport cost is zero

Bytes on the wire cost money (egress charges, cross-region transfer, cross-cloud). The cost can be invisible during development and dominant in production. A team that designs an event-streaming system without accounting for inter-region egress can produce a system whose cloud bill exceeds its salary budget.


#### The network is homogeneous

Different parts of your network have different bandwidth, latency, and reliability. A request that flows from a US-East customer to a US-East server is fast. The same code path from a Singapore customer to a US-East server is 200 ms slower, and the failure rate is different because Singapore's transit goes through more hops. Code that performs well in your test environment can perform badly under realistic traffic patterns.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

Many readers, on first seeing the Eight Fallacies, treat them as a checklist: "I have read the list; I have absorbed the lesson; I am ready to write distributed code." The fallacies do not work that way. The lesson is not that you should remember the list. The lesson is that single-machine intuition is wrong by default, and every distributed-systems decision should be examined for which fallacy it implicitly assumes.

A useful exercise: take any function in your distributed code and ask which of the eight assumptions it makes. Most functions make at least one. Most production bugs in distributed systems are one of the eight, slightly disguised.


### 2.2 CAP, Stated Precisely

Eric Brewer presented the CAP theorem as a conjecture at PODC 2000. Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved it in 2002. The slogan version of CAP says "pick two of consistency, availability, partition tolerance." This is misleading in two ways.

First, partition tolerance is not a choice. Networks partition. If you build a system that requires perfect network connectivity, your system is broken by definition the moment a single link drops a packet. The honest CAP statement is: when (not if) a partition occurs, you must choose between consistency and availability. The rest of the time, partition tolerance does not cost you anything.

Second, the "consistency" in CAP is not the loose word that databases use for "ACID-ish behavior." It is _linearizability_ , a specific and very strong property.


#### Linearizability

A system is linearizable if there exists a serial ordering of all operations consistent with real-time order, such that each operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between its invocation and its response.

The "consistent with real-time order" part is what makes it strong. If client A finishes a write at wall-clock time t1t_1t1​, and client B begins a read at wall-clock time t2>t1t_2 > t_1t2​>t1​ (the two clients can be on different machines), then B's read must see A's write (or any later write). The system must not be able to behave as if the write happened "after" the read.

A simpler way to think about it: a linearizable system behaves as if there were a single copy of the data, with all operations taking effect on that single copy in some order that respects real-time. The "as if" matters: the system can have many replicas internally, but its external behavior is indistinguishable from a single-copy system.


#### Availability

Availability in the CAP sense is also strict: every request to a non-failing node receives a non-error response, in bounded time. A node that responds with "I am not sure; please retry later" is not available in this sense.


#### The theorem

When a network partition occurs (one set of nodes cannot communicate with another set), a system cannot simultaneously be linearizable and available. The proof is a short construction: imagine two nodes on opposite sides of the partition, both available. Client A writes x=1x = 1x=1 to one side. Client B reads xxx from the other side. The two sides cannot communicate. The read either returns the old value (violating linearizability) or refuses to answer (violating availability). No third option exists.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### What CAP does not say

CAP does _not_ say:

* That you must "pick CP" or "pick AP" as a categorical property of your system.
* That the choice is the same for every operation. Spanner offers both strongly consistent reads and stale reads in the same database, served from the same replicas.
* That the choice matters when there is no partition.
* That "consistency" in any looser sense (read-your-writes, eventual, monotonic) is forbidden by CAP. CAP forbids only linearizability under partition with availability.

The narrow scope of CAP is the source of half the bad CAP discussions on the internet. Most workloads do not need linearizability for most operations. Many systems labeled "AP" provide stronger guarantees than the label implies; many systems labeled "CP" trade availability in subtle ways the label does not name.


### 2.3 PACELC: The Honest Extension

Daniel Abadi pointed out, around 2010, that CAP names only the partition case and ignores the much more common case: when the network is healthy. The trade-off in the healthy case is between latency and consistency.

PACELC: if Partition, then Availability or Consistency; Else, then Latency or Consistency.

The acronym is awkward but the point is sharp. CockroachDB during a partition is CP (it refuses writes to the partitioned side rather than serving stale data). CockroachDB during normal operation pays a latency cost for its consistency: a commit that needs to round-trip to a quorum of replicas across a region is slower than a commit that needs only to write to a local leader. Spanner pays the famous 7 ms of commit-wait (Chapter 13) to give linearizable timestamps via TrueTime.

DynamoDB during a partition is AP (the partitioned nodes continue to serve reads from their replicas, possibly stale). DynamoDB during normal operation has very low read latency because it does not coordinate reads with anything. Cassandra is similar; its tunable consistency lets you choose at request time whether you want speed or strict ordering.


#### PACELC in practice

The useful question for any system is: under PACELC, what does this system give up under partition, and what does it give up in normal operation? A PACELC summary for the systems you will meet in Part IV:

System | Under partition | Else (no partition)  
---|---|---  
Spanner | C (refuses writes minority side) | C with commit-wait latency  
CockroachDB | C (refuses writes minority side) | C with quorum-write latency  
TiDB / YugabyteDB | C | C with quorum-write latency  
DynamoDB | A (serves possibly stale reads) | L (low-latency reads, eventual consistency by default)  
Cassandra | tunable (per-request quorum) | tunable (L by default)  
FoundationDB | C | C, optimized for OLTP latency  
  
This table is more useful than the CAP table. CAP tells you what happens when things go wrong. PACELC tells you what your application pays _every day_ , which is usually what determines whether the system is right for your workload.


### 2.4 The Counter-Leaderboard-Inventory Workload

Throughout the book, three workloads will reappear as the test bed for consistency models. The three are the counter, the leaderboard, and the inventory commit. They differ in what they need from the system.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### The counter

A page-view counter on a popular article. Each "view" is one increment. The total is shown to a visitor with a delay of seconds or more. Tolerance for inconsistency: high. Tolerance for lost increments: medium (a 10% undercount in the displayed total is embarrassing but not catastrophic).

Suitable consistency: eventual is fine. Linearizability is overkill and would limit throughput by a large factor. A counter implemented as a CRDT (G-Counter, Chapter 16) on every replica, gossiping increments to converge, scales horizontally without coordination.


#### The leaderboard

The top 10 scores in a game, refreshed for all viewers within a few seconds. Each score submission is a write. The leaderboard is a read of the top-10. Tolerance for transient inconsistency: medium (different viewers may see different orderings for a few seconds). Tolerance for stale data after partition heal: low (everyone should converge on the same leaderboard within minutes).

Suitable consistency: causal consistency (Chapter 17) or strong-eventual. If two players A and B submit scores, and A's submission causally precedes B's (B saw A's appear before submitting), all viewers should eventually agree that A's appeared first.


#### The inventory commit

A purchase that decrements inventory by one. If two purchases race for the last item, exactly one must succeed. Tolerance for inconsistency: zero. Tolerance for partial failure: zero (we must not sell two items when one exists).

Suitable consistency: strong (linearizable) under partition. Either Spanner-style global linearizability or a Raft-replicated decrement (Chapter 9) on the inventory record. The latency cost is paid because the alternative (overselling) is unacceptable.

The three workloads recur because they show the spectrum: counter (eventual fine), leaderboard (causal needed), inventory (linearizable required). The mistake the inventory-as-a-CRDT engineer makes is using the technique that worked for the counter on a workload that does not tolerate convergence. The mistake the counter-on-Spanner engineer makes is paying linearizable latency for a workload that does not need it.


#### Common Misconception

Engineers sometimes treat consistency as a property of the system rather than a property of the request. Modern systems are much more flexible. Spanner offers stale reads with a configurable bound on staleness; Cassandra offers per-request quorum levels (ONE, QUORUM, ALL); CockroachDB offers `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` for bounded-staleness reads. The right question is not "is this system consistent?" but "what is the consistency of this specific operation, and what does it cost?"

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
### 2.5 PACELC Decision Procedure

When you are choosing between systems for a workload, the PACELC procedure is:

  1. **Classify the workload.** What does each operation need? Linearizable, causal, eventual?
  2. **Compute the latency budget.** What latency can the user (or downstream system) tolerate? Per-operation, p99, p999.
  3. **Estimate partition frequency.** A single-region system experiences partitions rarely (months between events). A cross-region system experiences cross-region partitions much more often (weeks). A geo-distributed cross-cloud system experiences them weekly or more.
  4. **Compute the partition-time cost.** When a partition occurs, what is the cost of unavailability versus the cost of stale reads? For an inventory system, unavailability is preferable to overselling. For a content-delivery system, stale reads are preferable to a blank page.
  5. **Pick the system whose PACELC profile matches.** For the workload, the latency budget, and the partition-time priority.

This procedure is what Chapter 11 will teach in depth as the "diagnostic method" for reading any distributed database in 30 minutes. The PACELC table is the summary.


### 2.6 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State each of Deutsch's Eight Fallacies in your own words, and give one example of code that quietly assumes each fallacy is true.

Hint

For each fallacy, find a code pattern. For "the network is reliable," code with no retry. For "latency is zero," a loop that does an RPC per element of a million-element array.

**Answer:**

_The network is reliable._ Example: `response = http.get(url); parse(response)` with no try/except, no timeout, no retry. Assumes the call always returns a parseable response.

_Latency is zero._ Example: `for item in million_items: total += rpc_lookup(item.id)`. Each call is 1 ms, so the loop takes 1000 seconds for a function that the engineer expected to take under a second. The same code with batched RPCs (1000 items per call) is 1000x faster.

_Bandwidth is infinite._ Example: a logging pipeline that sends each individual log line as a separate gRPC message to a centralized aggregator. The serialization overhead and per-message header cost dominate the actual log payload, and the aggregator's network saturates long before its CPU.

_The network is secure._ Example: an internal service that accepts any caller from the VPC because "the VPC is private." A compromised pod in the cluster can now act as any caller, because there is no per-caller authentication.

_Topology doesn't change._ Example: a configuration file with hardcoded IP addresses for service dependencies, no DNS, no service discovery. Works until a single node restarts on a new IP.

_There is one administrator._ Example: a Sunday-evening deploy that breaks because the network team rolled out a firewall change at 4 p.m. that no one in your team knew about. The change is permitted and operational from their view; your code happens to be the canary.

_Transport cost is zero._ Example: a cross-region data sync job that runs every five minutes "to keep the regions in sync." After the cloud bill arrives, the team discovers each sync transfers 50 GB across regions at 0.09 USD/GB. Monthly bill: many thousands of dollars for a feature no one is actively using.

_The network is homogeneous._ Example: a service whose p50 latency is 50 ms in test (all traffic from the same region) and 350 ms in production (some traffic from Asia to a US-East deployment). The code did not account for the realistic distribution of caller locations.

**Q2.** State CAP precisely. Then state what is wrong with the slogan version "pick two of consistency, availability, partition tolerance."

Hint

The precise statement is about what is forbidden in the presence of a partition. The slogan is wrong because partition tolerance is not a choice.

**Answer:** Precise statement: in a distributed system, in the presence of a network partition, the system cannot be both linearizable and available (where availability means "every non-failing node responds to every request with a non-error response in bounded time").

What is wrong with the slogan: it implies you can pick "consistency and availability without partition tolerance," but partitions happen whether you account for them or not. A system that "is not partition-tolerant" is not a system that experiences no partitions; it is a system that fails arbitrarily when partitions occur, which is worse than choosing in advance how to fail. The honest framing is: partitions are inevitable; under partition, choose between consistency and availability.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
The slogan also misleads by suggesting "consistency" is the loose database sense. CAP's consistency is linearizability, a much stronger property than transactional consistency or eventual consistency.

**Q3.** State PACELC. For each of (a) Spanner, (b) CockroachDB, (c) DynamoDB, (d) Cassandra with QUORUM reads/writes, give the PACELC classification.

Hint

PACELC: if Partition then Availability vs Consistency; Else then Latency vs Consistency. Each system is one of PA/EL, PA/EC, PC/EL, PC/EC.

**Answer:** PACELC: under Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else (no partition), choose Latency or Consistency.

(a) Spanner: PC/EC. Under partition, prefers consistency (the partitioned-out replicas refuse writes). Without partition, still consistent at the cost of commit-wait latency (the 7 ms TrueTime cost).

(b) CockroachDB: PC/EC. Under partition, the minority side refuses writes for affected keys. Without partition, commit latency includes quorum round-trip to replicas, which can be tens of milliseconds for cross-region deployments.

(c) DynamoDB: PA/EL. Under partition, serves possibly-stale reads from any replica. Without partition, reads are low-latency because they do not coordinate. (DynamoDB also offers strongly consistent reads at higher latency on request, which is a per-operation PACELC choice, not a global one.)

(d) Cassandra with QUORUM reads/writes: PC/EC for those specific operations. The QUORUM level requires majority of replicas to ack, so it refuses writes on the minority side of a partition, and pays quorum latency without partition. With LOCAL_QUORUM the picture changes; with ONE it becomes PA/EL. Cassandra is per-request, so the PACELC classification is per-operation.

**Q4.** A team is choosing between Spanner and DynamoDB for a flash-sale inventory system that will see 100,000 purchase requests per second for 60 seconds during a sale. The requirement is that no item is ever oversold. Using PACELC, walk through the decision.

Hint

"No item is ever oversold" is a linearizability requirement on the decrement-inventory operation. DynamoDB's default consistency is eventual; can it be coerced to linearizable for this operation, and what does that cost?

**Answer:** The "no oversold" requirement on the inventory decrement is a linearizability requirement. Under PACELC, both options can satisfy the requirement, but at different costs.

Spanner: linearizable by default. Each inventory decrement pays commit-wait latency (about 7 ms baseline, plus quorum round-trip). At 100,000 requests per second, Spanner needs enough shards (sharding the inventory across items) to spread the load. If the sale is for a single hot item, all decrements hit one shard and you are bounded by that shard's commit throughput, which is the limiting factor.

DynamoDB: eventually consistent by default. For "no oversell" you need conditional writes (`ConditionExpression`) plus strongly consistent reads. Conditional writes are atomic per-item at the partition layer; they will not oversell. The cost is the per-write conditional-check latency, which is higher than a normal eventual write but lower than Spanner's cross-region commit because it is single-region.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
PACELC says: both are PC under partition for this operation. The Else case favors DynamoDB on latency for the conditional-write path, especially if Spanner is multi-region. The Spanner case is cleaner if you need other strongly consistent reads in the same transaction (cart-and-inventory together).

Decision: if the sale is single-region and the only consistency requirement is per-item decrement, DynamoDB conditional writes win on latency and cost. If the sale spans regions or the system needs multi-item transactions (e.g., decrement inventory and increment user-purchases atomically), Spanner is the cleaner answer. A real team would also consider operational maturity, on-call expertise, and what the rest of the company already runs.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** You are evaluating a system that the documentation calls "AP." Read the documentation more carefully and identify three operations the system performs that are actually linearizable (i.e., it is not "AP" for those). Then identify the latency cost.

Hint

Most "AP" systems have a metadata path that needs linearizability: leader election, cluster membership, configuration. DynamoDB, for instance, has linearizable conditional writes.

**Answer:** Most "AP" systems are AP only for their data plane; their control plane needs strong consistency to function at all. Worked example for DynamoDB:

(a) Conditional writes via `ConditionExpression` are linearizable at the partition level. Cost: per-write latency includes a synchronous quorum check, which is higher than a default eventual put.

(b) Strongly consistent reads via `ConsistentRead=true` are linearizable. Cost: higher latency than eventual reads (DynamoDB documents roughly 2x), and they consume more capacity units.

(c) Stream metadata (cluster topology, shard assignment) is managed by a strongly consistent control plane invisible to the user. The user does not pay latency on it directly, but operations during a control-plane change can see brief unavailability.

For Cassandra: lightweight transactions (LWT) using `IF NOT EXISTS` or `IF` clauses are linearizable via Paxos. Cost: dramatically higher latency than non-LWT writes (often 4x to 10x), because the Paxos round-trip happens per-write.

For Riak: strong-consistency buckets (when enabled) are linearizable. Cost: each operation pays a coordination round-trip; throughput drops by an order of magnitude compared to eventual buckets.

The lesson: every "AP" system has a CP corner. Knowing which operations sit in which corner is more useful than the system-level label.

**Q2.** Your colleague claims "we use CockroachDB, so we are linearizable for free." Identify three operations or configurations in CockroachDB that are _not_ linearizable by default, and explain when this matters.

Hint

CockroachDB has `AS OF SYSTEM TIME`, follower reads, and the default `SNAPSHOT` isolation level used to be weaker than serializable in older versions. Each has a non-linearizable corner.

**Answer:**

(a) `AS OF SYSTEM TIME` reads are bounded-staleness reads from any replica. They are not linearizable; they explicitly return data from a past consistent snapshot. They are very fast (no leader hop) and useful for analytics. Misuse: using them for inventory checks or balance reads in a transaction that needs the latest state.

(b) Follower reads via `AS OF SYSTEM TIME follower_read_timestamp()` read from the nearest replica with bounded staleness. Same trade-off as above. Useful for global low-latency reads of slowly-changing data.

(c) The transaction priority interaction with `CONCURRENTLY` operations can produce subtle non-linearizable behavior across statements in different sessions if you misread the isolation guarantees. CockroachDB defaults to serializable isolation, which is the strongest of the SQL isolation levels, but serializable is not the same as linearizable across sessions; serializable orders transactions in some valid order, while linearizable orders them consistent with real-time. For many workloads the difference does not matter; for "the read in session B begins after the write in session A returns to session A" expectations, the difference can matter.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
When it matters: any read where the application logic assumes "I am seeing the latest data" must use a fresh read at the leader, not a follower read and not `AS OF SYSTEM TIME`. The error of using a stale read where a linearizable read is needed is a class of bug that linearizable-by-default systems do not prevent automatically.

**Q3.** Walk through the counter-leaderboard-inventory workload from §2.4 and explain why each one's consistency requirement is what it is. Then propose a single system that could serve all three. What are the trade-offs of choosing one system versus three specialized systems?

Hint

Spanner can serve all three (linearizable for inventory, eventual via stale reads for counter, causal-ish via session reads for leaderboard). The trade-off is operational simplicity versus latency cost.

**Answer:**

_Counter:_ eventual is fine because the user-visible cost of inconsistency (the displayed view count is off by a few seconds) is much less than the system cost of linearizable counting (every increment must coordinate). A CRDT-based counter or eventually-consistent put-with-merge serves this workload at near-zero coordination cost.

_Leaderboard:_ causal because two players' submissions have a causal relationship if one player saw the other's score before submitting. All viewers should eventually see the same ordering, but a few seconds of disagreement is acceptable. Stronger-than-eventual but weaker-than-linearizable.

_Inventory:_ linearizable because overselling is unacceptable. The cost (per-decrement coordination) is paid because the alternative is worse.

One system that serves all three: Spanner. Use strongly consistent transactions for inventory, eventual-consistency stale reads for the counter, and bounded-staleness reads for the leaderboard. The trade-off:

* Pro: one operational footprint, one query language, one access-control model.
* Pro: cross-workload transactions become trivial (decrement inventory and update leaderboard atomically).
* Con: Spanner's commit-wait latency is paid on every write, even on the workloads that do not need it.
* Con: throughput per shard is bounded by the consensus round-trip, so the counter cannot scale as high on Spanner as on a CRDT-based counter.

Three specialized systems (Redis for counter, Cassandra for leaderboard, Spanner for inventory) achieve higher peak throughput on each workload at the cost of operational complexity, cross-system consistency problems, and the engineering cost of three separate observability and on-call playbooks. The right answer depends on scale, team size, and how much cross-workload work the application does.

**Q4.** Pick a system in your stack and write a one-page PACELC profile for it, naming what it does under partition and what it costs in normal operation. Be specific about which operations are linearizable and which are not.

Hint

Use the table format from §2.3. For each operation type the system supports, name its PACELC classification.

**Answer:** This is the exercise the rest of Part IV will train you on. A worked example for Redis Cluster:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
Redis Cluster: under partition, the partitioned-out nodes refuse writes for hash slots they no longer own (configurable via `cluster-require-full-coverage`). Normal-operation reads from a replica are not linearizable; they are eventually consistent with the master. Writes to the master are not durable until replicated; under failover, recently-acknowledged writes can be lost (this is documented; see the Jepsen Redis analysis for the details, Chapter 18).

Per operation:

Operation | Partition | Normal-op cost  
---|---|---  
Master write | PC (write fails minority) | L (single-node) but not durable  
Replica read | PA (serves stale) | L (very fast)  
`SET NX EX` (lock) | PA (lock can be split) | L, but unsafe under partition (Chapter 18)  
Lua script | PC (atomic on one master) | L per master, but scoped to one slot  
  
The PACELC profile makes it clear which operations are safe under which conditions, and where the system's defaults will surprise you. This is the level of detail Chapter 11 will teach you to produce for any system in 30 minutes.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "CAP is obsolete in 2026; PACELC is the only framing engineers need." Use evidence from at least two production systems.

**Discussion:** Both framings have a place. CAP names the choice the system designer must make about the rare-but-real partition case. PACELC names the choice the application user pays every day. Neither alone is sufficient.

The defense of "CAP is obsolete" goes: in modern cloud deployments, partitions are short (seconds, not hours), and the latency-vs-consistency choice in normal operation dominates user experience. For 99.9% of seconds, PACELC is what matters; CAP only enters during incident response.

The refutation: when a partition does occur, the CAP behavior is what determines whether your system silently corrupts data, refuses requests cleanly, or serves stale answers. The choice has to be made in advance. Production systems that did not think through CAP have caused outages large enough to be named after them.

A useful synthesis: CAP is the worst-case behavior; PACELC is the everyday behavior. Both belong in any serious system evaluation, with PACELC getting more design attention because it dominates everyday cost, and CAP getting more design attention for safety-critical workloads where the partition-case behavior is itself the requirement.

Worked example: Spanner is PC/EC. Spanner's design pays heavy normal-operation latency (commit-wait) so that under partition, it remains consistent. For Google ads (the original Spanner workload), this trade is correct because monetary data must be exactly right under all conditions. For a social-feed product, the same trade would be wrong; the partition behavior should be "show what we have," not "refuse to serve."

**Q2.** An LLM, asked "should I pick a CP or AP database for my online store," outputs a confident recommendation in three paragraphs. Without specifying which the model picked, identify the questions the model failed to ask, and explain why getting the answer "right" without asking them is a luckier outcome than getting the answer "wrong."

**Discussion:** The questions the model failed to ask include:

* What operations does the store perform? Inventory commit and payment commit need linearizability; product browsing and review reading do not.
* What is the deployment footprint? Single-region versus multi-region changes the latency profile dramatically.
* What is the team's operational maturity? A team that has not run a distributed database before will get more value from a managed PostgreSQL than from any "ideal" distributed system, because operational failures will dominate.
* What is the read/write ratio? A 1000:1 read/write workload tolerates very different storage choices than a 1:1.
* What is the cost budget? Spanner is expensive; DynamoDB is cheap on small workloads and expensive on hot keys; CockroachDB is cheaper than Spanner but needs operational expertise.
* What does the team need to integrate with? An ecosystem of existing Postgres-based tooling makes a Postgres-compatible system (Aurora DSQL, CockroachDB, Neon) cheaper to adopt than a NoSQL alternative.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 2: The Eight Fallacies, CAP, and PACELC
blocks.src:
A model that gives an answer without asking any of this is, at best, lucky. The right answer for a single-region Shopify-style store is probably PostgreSQL + read replicas; the right answer for a Stripe-style global payment system is probably Spanner or TigerBeetle. The right reasoning path goes through the questions. An answer without the reasoning path is a value the team cannot defend, cannot extend, and cannot debug when the workload changes.

The deeper observation: distributed-systems decisions are not the kind of decision where you can outsource the reasoning. The reasoning _is_ the decision. An LLM-generated answer that happens to be correct gives the team no understanding of why, no ability to evaluate a future change, and no defense when the assumptions shift.


### Chapter Summary

Deutsch's Eight Fallacies name the single-machine intuitions that produce most distributed-systems bugs. The fallacies are not a checklist to memorize; they are the categories of assumption to audit in every piece of distributed code. Chapter 21 will revisit the network-reliability fallacy as cascading failures; Chapter 18 will revisit the security and "one administrator" fallacies as lock-and-coordination bugs.

CAP, precisely stated, says that under network partition you cannot have both linearizability and availability. The slogan version ("pick two") is misleading because partition tolerance is not a choice. CAP's "consistency" is linearizability, a much stronger property than the loose database sense of the word.

PACELC extends CAP to the case CAP ignores: when there is no partition. PACELC names the trade-off between latency and consistency in normal operation, which is what your application pays every day. The PACELC profile of a system is more practically useful than its CAP label.

The counter-leaderboard-inventory workload from §2.4 will return throughout the book. Each represents a point on the consistency spectrum: counter (eventual fine), leaderboard (causal needed), inventory (linearizable required). Knowing which workload needs which consistency is a more useful skill than knowing which database is "CP" or "AP."

Chapter 3 takes the first lie, time, and develops the protocols (Lamport, vector, HLC, TrueTime) that let you reason about ordering across machines without lying. The Spanner commit-wait latency we mentioned in this chapter has its full explanation in Chapter 3; the CockroachDB HLC-based MVCC has its full explanation in Chapter 13.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 3: Time, Order, and the Lying Clocks
blocks.src:
An LLM, asked to write a chat-message ordering function, produces:
    
    
    def display_in_order(messages):
        return sorted(messages, key=lambda m: m.timestamp)
    

> Illustrative pseudocode; the bug is structural (the wrong primitive), not syntactic.

The function is short. It looks right. It will, in production, occasionally display a reply before the message it replies to. This chapter is about why, and what the working alternatives are.

The hard truth: there is no global "now" in a distributed system. When two events happen on two machines and you want to know which came first, the timestamp on each event tells you a story that may or may not match reality. The story comes from a clock, and the clock is lying to you in a specific, structured way that you can defend against if you understand it.


### 3.1 NTP and Why It Is Not Enough

NTP (Network Time Protocol) is the mechanism that keeps machine clocks roughly synchronized. NTP works by querying a small set of time servers, measuring round-trip latency, and slewing the local clock toward the consensus.

On a healthy LAN with a Stratum-2 NTP server nearby, machines stay synchronized to within a few milliseconds. On a wide-area network or a noisy link, the bound is closer to tens of milliseconds. On a machine whose NTP daemon has failed silently (the daemon is not running, the configuration is wrong, the upstream server is unreachable), the local clock drifts at the hardware's rate, which on a typical server is on the order of seconds per day.

The implications are subtle. NTP gives you bounded _expected_ drift; it does not give you bounded _guaranteed_ drift unless you actively measure and react. A server with NTP misconfigured for a week can be many seconds off its peers, while still serving requests as if healthy.

Two more sharp edges:

* **NTP can move time backward.** When a large drift is detected, NTP can step the clock backward by hundreds of milliseconds in one jump. Code that measures duration with `t2 - t1` where `t1` is from before the step and `t2` is from after will return a negative duration.
* **Leap seconds.** Once every few years, UTC inserts a leap second. Different systems handle it differently (smear, step, repeat). The Cloudflare 2017 leap-second incident is the canonical case study; their DNS service experienced negative durations that propagated into a sort comparison, causing data structures to break.

The disciplined practice in modern distributed systems is to assume clock skew can be up to a known bound (typically configured at 250 ms or 500 ms in production systems), to monitor for NTP health, and to never write code that depends on `wall_clock_a < wall_clock_b` for ordering events from different machines.


#### Monotonic clocks

A separate clock, the _monotonic_ clock, is the right tool for measuring duration on a single machine. Monotonic clocks never go backward (they are not adjusted by NTP) and never jump forward. They are not tied to wall-clock time; their values are meaningful only as differences. Most modern languages expose both: in Python `time.time()` is wall, `time.monotonic()` is monotonic; in Go `time.Now()` returns a value that carries both internally.

The rule: any code that measures "how long did X take" should use monotonic time. Any code that records "when did X happen" must use wall time but recognize the limits.
