They have voted (and are holding locks), they cannot decide on their own (they do not know what the other participants voted), and they cannot abort (the coordinator might have committed before crashing).

This blocking is not just "lock contention." It is a deeper structural issue: 2PC reduces consensus to a single coordinator, and the coordinator becomes a single point of failure for liveness. The participants are blocked until the coordinator recovers, which may be never.

3PC (3-phase commit) was proposed to fix this, but 3PC also fails under network partitions; it is non-blocking only under specific failure models that production networks do not satisfy.

The real fix is _replicated coordinators_ : the coordinator's state is itself replicated via consensus (Raft or Paxos), so any coordinator-state is recoverable from the consensus log. This is the Spanner / CockroachDB / Percolator pattern (Chapter 13).

An LLM that answers "lock contention" without mentioning the blocking failure mode has missed the central reason 2PC is not used as a general consensus primitive. The blocking failure mode is what makes 2PC unsuitable as a building block; lock contention is a separate (real but less fundamental) concern.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 7: Why Consensus Is Hard
blocks.src:
The deeper observation: a lot of LLM-generated explanations of distributed protocols name surface symptoms (lock contention, latency) without naming the structural reason (blocking on coordinator failure, lack of quorum intersection). The structural reasons are what determine which protocol is right; the surface symptoms are what determine when you notice the problem.


### Chapter Summary

Consensus is the problem of getting a set of processes to agree on a value despite some of them crashing. The three properties (agreement, validity, termination) are the canonical statement. FLP impossibility says deterministic protocols cannot achieve all three under pure asynchrony with one crash; the modern escape hatches are partial synchrony, randomization, and failure detectors.

Safety properties ("bad things never happen") are guaranteed always by modern consensus protocols. Liveness properties ("good things eventually happen") are guaranteed only after the network stabilizes. The Crescent multi-region commit log uses Raft, which is safe under all network conditions but may pause during partitions.

The three properties map to specific design choices in real protocols: quorum intersection for agreement, structural validity from leader proposals, partial-synchrony plus heartbeats for termination. Reading any new consensus paper through this lens makes the structure visible.

Chapter 8 takes the first canonical protocol, Paxos, and walks it step by step. Lamport's 1989 paper (rewritten in plain English in 2001) is one of the most influential papers in distributed systems. Multi-Paxos extends single-decree Paxos to a sequence of decisions, which is the real form deployed in production (Spanner, Megastore). Chapter 9 takes Raft, which Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout designed in 2014 explicitly to be more understandable than Paxos.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
In 1989, Leslie Lamport submitted a paper titled "The Part-Time Parliament" to ACM Transactions on Computer Systems. It described a fictional Greek island whose part-time legislators passed decrees through an elaborate ritual involving messengers, ledgers, and quorums. The paper was reviewed unfavorably (one reviewer suggested it was a joke), and Lamport withdrew it. He published it eventually in 1998.

The protocol described in the paper is Paxos, and it is the most influential consensus algorithm in the history of distributed systems. Google built Chubby (the basis of Spanner) on Paxos. ZooKeeper's ZAB is a Paxos variant. The protocol is famously hard to implement correctly; Lamport himself rewrote the explanation in 2001 as "Paxos Made Simple," and it is still hard.

This chapter teaches Paxos in the form it usually shows up: single-decree Paxos (agreeing on one value) and Multi-Paxos (agreeing on a sequence of values). The point is not to memorize the messages; it is to understand the structural invariants that make Paxos safe. Raft (Chapter 9) is easier to implement but follows the same skeleton.


### 8.1 The Setting

A set of NNN processes, each playing one or more of three roles:

* **Proposer** : tries to get a value chosen.
* **Acceptor** : votes on proposals; persists state across crashes.
* **Learner** : discovers and learns the chosen value.

A single process can play all three roles. The protocol works for any N≥2f+1N \ge 2f + 1N≥2f+1 where fff is the number of crash failures tolerated. The classical setting is N=3,f=1N = 3, f = 1N=3,f=1 or N=5,f=2N = 5, f = 2N=5,f=2.

The goal: choose a single value. The protocol must guarantee:

* **Validity** : only a proposed value can be chosen.
* **Agreement** : only one value is chosen (no two acceptors disagree on the chosen value once the protocol completes).
* **Termination** : with no failures and a stable leader, the protocol terminates.


### 8.2 Why the Naive Protocols Fail

Before Paxos, consider what a naive protocol might do.

**Naive Protocol 1** : a single designated proposer sends its value to all acceptors. All acceptors store the value. Done.

Problem: the proposer can crash before delivering to all acceptors. Some acceptors have the value; some do not. There is no agreement on what is chosen.

**Naive Protocol 2** : a single designated proposer sends its value; waits for majority of acks. Done.

Problem: the proposer can crash mid-protocol. The remaining acceptors do not know whether the proposer committed (sent acks to client) or aborted. A new proposer cannot know whether to propose a new value or to retry the old one.

**Naive Protocol 3** : any proposer can propose; acceptors accept the first proposal they see.

Problem: two proposers can each have their value accepted by a non-overlapping subset; no value has majority; no agreement.

Paxos solves all of these by introducing two phases (prepare, accept) and using _quorum intersection_ plus _ballot numbers_ to ensure that once a value is chosen, no other value can be chosen.


### 8.3 The Single-Decree Paxos Protocol

The protocol has two phases. Each phase has a request and a response.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
#### Phase 1: Prepare

A proposer that wants to propose a value picks a _ballot number_ bbb. Ballot numbers are uniquely assigned (e.g., (counter, proposer_id) with lexicographic order) and monotonically increasing over time.

The proposer sends `PREPARE(b)` to every acceptor.

Each acceptor, upon receiving `PREPARE(b)`:

* If bbb is less than or equal to the highest ballot bmaxb_{max}bmax​ the acceptor has seen, ignore (or reply NACK).
* Otherwise, update bmax←bb_{max} \leftarrow bbmax​←b, and reply `PROMISE(b, accepted_ballot, accepted_value)` where `accepted_ballot` and `accepted_value` are whatever the acceptor most recently _accepted_ (possibly null).

The promise commits the acceptor to: "I will not accept any proposal with ballot less than bbb."


#### Phase 2: Accept

The proposer collects `PROMISE` responses. If it receives promises from a majority of acceptors, it can proceed.

The proposer's value for the accept phase:

* If any of the received promises contained a non-null `accepted_value`, the proposer must pick the value from the promise with the _highest_ `accepted_ballot`.
* Otherwise (all promises had null `accepted_value`), the proposer picks its own original value.

This is the safety property in action: any value already "in flight" (accepted by some acceptor) must be the value the new ballot proposes. The proposer cannot ignore prior accepted values; it must adopt them.

The proposer sends `ACCEPT(b, v)` to all acceptors.

Each acceptor, upon receiving `ACCEPT(b, v)`:

* If bbb is less than bmaxb_{max}bmax​, ignore.
* Otherwise, persist (b,v)(b, v)(b,v) as `accepted_ballot, accepted_value`, and reply `ACCEPTED(b, v)`.

When the proposer collects `ACCEPTED` from a majority, the value vvv is _chosen_.


#### Learning

Once a value is chosen, learners must learn it. The simplest approach: when an acceptor accepts a value with majority support, it tells the learners. Optimizations exist (a designated learner; piggyback on protocol messages).


### 8.4 Why Paxos Is Safe

The safety argument has three parts.

**Part 1: ballot numbers are total-ordered.** Each ballot is unique and ballots are monotonically issued. The protocol's behavior depends only on ballot order, not on real time.

**Part 2: quorum intersection.** Any two majorities of NNN acceptors intersect in at least one acceptor. (For N=3N = 3N=3, any two sets of 2 share at least 1; for N=5N = 5N=5, any two sets of 3 share at least 1.) This is the foundational property: any decision made by one majority is "remembered" by some acceptor in any other majority.

**Part 3: the accept rule preserves prior decisions.** When a proposer sends `ACCEPT`, the value it proposes is constrained by Phase 1's responses. If any acceptor in the prepare quorum had accepted a prior value, the new value must match (it must adopt the highest-ballot value). This means: once a value has been chosen (accepted by a majority), any subsequent ballot's prepare phase will see that value in some response (by quorum intersection), and must propose it.

Together: once vvv is chosen at ballot bbb, no later ballot b′>bb' > bb′>b can choose a different value. Any prepare for b′b'b′ intersects the majority that accepted vvv; the prepare response carries vvv (along with ballot bbb); the proposer must propose vvv.

This is the agreement property: any chosen value remains the chosen value forever, regardless of how many later ballots run.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

A common misconception is that Paxos elects a leader and the leader proposes values. Single-decree Paxos has no concept of leader. Any process can propose at any time; the protocol's safety holds even when multiple proposers run concurrently. The proposers may interfere with each other (cause restarts and termination delays), but they cannot violate safety.

Multi-Paxos (next section) introduces a leader for efficiency, but the leader is an optimization, not a safety requirement.


### 8.5 Multi-Paxos

Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value. State-machine replication needs a sequence of values (one per slot in the replicated log). The naive extension is to run an independent Paxos instance per slot, but the cost (two phases per slot) is high.

Multi-Paxos: elect a stable leader who runs Phase 1 once for an entire range of slots, then runs only Phase 2 for each subsequent slot.

The structure:

  1. A would-be leader picks a high ballot number bbb.
  2. The leader runs Phase 1 (`PREPARE(b)`) for slots starting at the current log end.
  3. Acceptors respond with their highest accepted value for each slot.
  4. The leader determines the value for any "in-flight" slots (slots where someone had already accepted) and continues normally for fresh slots.
  5. For each new value the leader wants to commit, it skips Phase 1 and just runs Phase 2 (`ACCEPT(b, v)`) for the next slot.

The optimization saves a round-trip per decision: instead of 2 round-trips (prepare + accept), there is 1 (accept). Phase 1 is amortized across many decisions.

Stable leadership is critical: if leadership changes frequently, Phase 1 must run each time, defeating the optimization. Modern systems (Spanner, etcd-via-Raft) have leadership-stability of minutes to hours, so the per-decision cost is one round-trip.


#### Leader election in Multi-Paxos

The leader election is itself a Paxos instance (or a degenerate equivalent). When a process suspects the current leader is dead (heartbeat timeout), it starts a new ballot. If multiple processes start ballots simultaneously, they interfere, and the protocol may livelock until one ballot "wins" (gets phase 1 majority first).

The randomized timeout pattern (used in Raft) avoids livelock by randomizing the heartbeat timeout, making simultaneous election starts statistically unlikely.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
### 8.6 Why Paxos Is Hard to Implement

Lamport's "Paxos Made Simple" paper is 14 pages. The actual implementations are thousands of lines. The gap is in the operational details:

* **Persistent state** : acceptors must persist bmaxb_{max}bmax​, accepted_ballotaccepted\\_ballotaccepted_ballot, accepted_valueaccepted\\_valueaccepted_value across crashes. Loss of this state breaks safety.
* **Reconfiguration** : changing the set of acceptors (adding or removing nodes) must itself be done via Paxos to avoid two competing configurations. The "joint consensus" protocol is subtle.
* **Snapshotting** : the log grows without bound; periodic snapshots truncate it. The snapshot must be consistent with the log state.
* **Stable storage discipline** : fsync after every accept; if you skip fsync, an acceptor can lose its accepted value and break safety.
* **Network partition handling** : if the leader is partitioned from a majority, the minority side cannot make progress. The leader must step down when it loses majority contact.
* **Multi-Paxos optimizations** : pipelining, batching, leader-lease leases — each has subtle interactions.

Google's Megastore paper (2011) and Spanner paper (2012) describe what production Paxos looks like; the level of detail is sobering. Implementations like libpaxos exist but are not widely used; most teams either use a higher-level system (Spanner, etcd) or implement Raft instead.

The folklore: "There are very few correct implementations of Paxos in the world." When Google migrated from Chubby (Paxos-based) to its successors, they preserved Paxos because the engineers had built deep expertise in operating it; new teams use Raft for the same reasons Diego Ongaro designed it.


### 8.7 The Paxos Family

Many protocols are "Paxos with extensions":

* **Fast Paxos** : skip Phase 1 in the common case; uses a larger quorum (3/4 instead of 1/2 + 1). Faster when uncontended; can be slower or unsafe under contention.
* **Generalized Paxos** : allows concurrent non-conflicting proposals to be ordered. Higher throughput for workloads with commutative operations.
* **Cheap Paxos** : separates "live" acceptors (active in the protocol) from "auxiliary" acceptors (consulted only during failures). Lower steady-state cost.
* **Egalitarian Paxos (EPaxos)** : leaderless; every replica can propose, and conflicts are resolved per-proposal. Higher throughput; more complex to reason about.
* **Flexible Paxos** (Heidi Howard's 2016 quorum flexibility work): generalizes the quorum requirement. The prepare quorum and accept quorum need only _intersect_ , not both be majorities. This lets the system tune the trade-off (smaller accept quorums for faster commits).

Modern production systems mostly use Multi-Paxos with leader leases. The leader lease is an addition: the leader holds a time-bounded "lease" granted by the acceptors; while the lease holds, the leader can serve linearizable reads without consensus rounds (the lease guarantees no other leader exists during the lease window). Spanner and CockroachDB both use lease-based reads as a major performance optimization.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
### 8.8 Worked Example

Three acceptors A1,A2,A3A_1, A_2, A_3A1​,A2​,A3​; one proposer.

**Step 1** : Proposer sends `PREPARE(b=10)` to all three.

**Step 2** : All three acceptors have bmax=0b_{max} = 0bmax​=0 (initial), so they accept the prepare. Each sets bmax=10b_{max} = 10bmax​=10 and responds `PROMISE(10, null, null)`.

**Step 3** : Proposer collects 3 promises (a majority). All accepted_value are null, so the proposer uses its own value v="hello"v = \text{"hello"}v="hello".

**Step 4** : Proposer sends `ACCEPT(b=10, v=\text{"hello"})` to all three.

**Step 5** : All three accept. They set accepted_ballot = 10, accepted_value = "hello", and respond `ACCEPTED(10, "hello")`.

**Step 6** : Proposer receives 3 accepted responses (majority). The value "hello" is now _chosen_.

Now suppose a second proposer (perhaps because the first crashed) starts a new ballot:

**Step 7** : Second proposer sends `PREPARE(b=20)`.

**Step 8** : Acceptors have bmax=10b_{max} = 10bmax​=10. They accept the prepare. Each responds `PROMISE(20, 10, "hello")` (the previously accepted value, with its ballot).

**Step 9** : Second proposer collects 3 promises. All carry the accepted value "hello" with ballot 10. By the accept rule, the second proposer must propose "hello" (the highest accepted ballot's value).

**Step 10** : Second proposer sends `ACCEPT(b=20, v="hello")`. Acceptors accept, updating their state.

The chosen value remains "hello." Any future ballot will also see "hello" in prepare responses (by quorum intersection) and will propose "hello." The protocol is safe.

If the second proposer had tried to propose a different value (e.g., "world"), it would have been forced by the protocol to propose "hello" instead. The proposer's "desire" does not override the safety invariant.


### 8.9 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Describe Paxos Phase 1 (prepare) and Phase 2 (accept). What does each phase guarantee?

Hint

Phase 1: get permission to propose; learn any prior accepted values. Phase 2: propose and have a majority accept.

**Answer:**

_Phase 1 (Prepare):_ The proposer picks a ballot number bbb and sends `PREPARE(b)` to all acceptors. Acceptors that have not promised any higher ballot respond `PROMISE(b, accepted_ballot, accepted_value)`. The promise is a commitment by the acceptor not to accept any future proposal with ballot less than bbb.

What Phase 1 guarantees: if the proposer receives promises from a majority, then no future proposal with ballot less than bbb can be chosen. Additionally, the proposer now knows the highest accepted value (if any) at each acceptor in the majority; this constrains what it can propose.

_Phase 2 (Accept):_ The proposer picks a value (either the highest-ballot accepted value from Phase 1, or its own if no value was accepted) and sends `ACCEPT(b, v)` to all acceptors. Acceptors that have not promised a higher ballot accept.

What Phase 2 guarantees: if the proposer receives accepts from a majority, the value is _chosen_. By quorum intersection, any subsequent ballot's Phase 1 will see this accepted value (in the majority's promises) and will be forced to propose it.

Together, the two phases guarantee that once a value is chosen, all subsequent ballots will agree on it. This is the agreement property.

**Q2.** Why does the proposer in Phase 2 have to use the highest-ballot accepted value from Phase 1 responses, rather than its own original value?

Hint

If a previous ballot had accepted a value, that value might be chosen; the new proposer cannot overwrite it.

**Answer:** Suppose a previous ballot had partially accepted a value vprevv_{prev}vprev​: some acceptors had accepted, but the proposer crashed before learning whether a majority had accepted. From the system's perspective, vprevv_{prev}vprev​ might be chosen (if a majority happens to have accepted) or might not be (if fewer accepted).

If the new proposer ignores vprevv_{prev}vprev​ and proposes its own vnewv_{new}vnew​, and the protocol were to choose vnewv_{new}vnew​, then both vprevv_{prev}vprev​ and vnewv_{new}vnew​ might be considered chosen by different observers, violating agreement.

The accept rule (proposer must adopt the highest-ballot accepted value seen in Phase 1) prevents this. Any value already accepted by some acceptor (even if not yet a majority) is "in flight" and might already be chosen. The new ballot must adopt it to avoid the safety violation.

Once the new ballot's Phase 2 completes with vprevv_{prev}vprev​, the value is unambiguously chosen. Any future ballot will see vprevv_{prev}vprev​ and propose it. The system has converged on a single chosen value.

**Q3.** What is Multi-Paxos and how does it improve on single-decree Paxos for state machine replication?

Hint

Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value; SMR needs a sequence. Multi-Paxos amortizes Phase 1 over many decisions.

**Answer:** Multi-Paxos extends single-decree Paxos to agree on a sequence of values (one per log slot), as needed for state-machine replication. The improvement: a stable leader runs Phase 1 once for many slots, then runs only Phase 2 per slot.

Specifically:

(a) A leader is elected (via a Paxos instance or an equivalent mechanism). The leader holds the role until it crashes or is suspected.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
(b) The leader runs Phase 1 once at the start of its tenure for all future slots. This is the "prepare for slots [current_slot, infinity)" pattern.

(c) For each subsequent value to commit, the leader runs only Phase 2 (ACCEPT). Acceptors that promised the leader's ballot will accept.

The cost per decision is one round-trip (ACCEPT plus ACCEPTED) instead of two (PREPARE + PROMISE + ACCEPT + ACCEPTED). For a stable leader serving many decisions, the amortization is significant.

If leadership is unstable (frequent re-elections), each re-election costs a Phase 1. Practical Multi-Paxos systems aim for leadership stability of minutes to hours.

**Q4.** Why is Paxos famously hard to implement correctly? Name three operational concerns.

Hint

Persistent state, reconfiguration, snapshotting, fsync discipline, multi-paxos optimizations.

**Answer:** Paxos is hard for several operational reasons:

(a) **Persistent state discipline** : acceptors must persist bmaxb_{max}bmax​, accepted_ballotaccepted\\_ballotaccepted_ballot, accepted_valueaccepted\\_valueaccepted_value to durable storage _before_ responding to prepare or accept messages. If an acceptor loses this state (due to disk failure, fsync omission, or filesystem corruption), it can "forget" its prior promises and accept conflicting values, violating safety.

(b) **Reconfiguration** : changing the set of acceptors (adding or removing nodes) cannot be done casually because two different configurations could each form a "majority" with no overlap. The standard solution is "joint consensus" or "alpha-paxos" patterns, but implementing these correctly is subtle.

(c) **Snapshotting and log truncation** : the Paxos log grows without bound; production systems must snapshot the state machine and truncate the log. The snapshot must be consistent with the log state at the snapshot point; truncating too aggressively can leave a recovering replica without enough log to catch up.

Three more (any of which has caused production failures):

(d) **Stable leadership maintenance** : Multi-Paxos relies on stable leadership; if leadership churns due to network instability, every churn costs a Phase 1 round and may pause the cluster.

(e) **Read consistency** : serving linearizable reads requires either a consensus round (slow) or a lease-based shortcut (faster, but the lease implementation is delicate).

(f) **Membership change during outage** : removing a failed node during a partition is dangerous; the partition may heal and the "removed" node may resurface, leading to a configuration discrepancy.

The cumulative effect: Paxos implementations are typically thousands of lines of careful code. Bugs in any of the above can cause silent safety violations that surface as data corruption months later. The folk wisdom that "there are few correct Paxos implementations" is not hyperbole.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A team is implementing single-decree Paxos for a leader-election service. They have 5 acceptors. Walk through a scenario where two proposers (A and B) start ballots concurrently. Trace the protocol to show that exactly one value is eventually chosen.

Hint

The proposer with the higher ballot wins. The other proposer's prepare or accept fails, and it must retry with a higher ballot.

**Answer:** Setup: 5 acceptors. Proposer A wants to propose value "Anya"; Proposer B wants to propose "Olamide".

**Concurrent prepare:**

* A sends `PREPARE(b=10)` to all 5.
* B sends `PREPARE(b=20)` to all 5.

Assume B's prepare reaches acceptors before A's at acceptors 1, 2, 3 (network races). Acceptors 1, 2, 3 set bmax=20b_{max} = 20bmax​=20 and respond `PROMISE(20, null, null)` to B. Acceptors 4, 5 receive A's first; they set bmax=10b_{max} = 10bmax​=10 and respond `PROMISE(10, null, null)` to A. Then they receive B's, set bmax=20b_{max} = 20bmax​=20, and respond `PROMISE(20, null, null)` to B.

A's situation: A has 2 promises (from acceptors 4, 5 only) at ballot 10. A is short of majority (needs 3).

B's situation: B has 5 promises at ballot 20.

**B's accept:**

* B sends `ACCEPT(20, "Olamide")` to all 5.
* All 5 accept. B receives 5 acceptedmessages. Value "Olamide" is chosen.

**A's retry:**

* A's prepare(10) failed (only 2 promises). A picks a higher ballot, say 30.
* A sends `PREPARE(b=30)`.
* All 5 acceptors have bmax=20b_{max} = 20bmax​=20 and accepted_value = "Olamide" (with accepted_ballot = 20). They respond `PROMISE(30, 20, "Olamide")`.
* A receives majority promises. By the accept rule, A must propose "Olamide" (the value from the highest accepted_ballot).
* A sends `ACCEPT(30, "Olamide")`. All 5 accept (they already have "Olamide" at ballot 20; updating to ballot 30 with the same value).
* A "chose" "Olamide" — but the value was already chosen at ballot 20.

The system has converged on a single value, "Olamide." A's original desire to propose "Anya" was overridden by the safety rule.

**Q2.** A Multi-Paxos cluster has 5 nodes. The current leader's network connection to 3 of the 4 other nodes degrades; only one peer remains reachable. What does the cluster do?

Hint

The leader can no longer get majority for accepts. Followers' election timers fire. A new leader is elected on the majority side.

**Answer:** The current leader can no longer get majority for accept messages (it can only reach 1 other node; a majority requires 3 of 5). New accepts time out. The leader cannot commit.

Meanwhile, the 3 unreachable followers no longer receive heartbeats from the leader. Their election timers fire (typically after a few hundred milliseconds to seconds). One of them starts a new ballot (prepare with a higher ballot number).

The new ballot's prepare reaches the majority side (the 3 unreachable followers can communicate with each other). The 3 acceptors on the majority side promise. The new leader has 3 promises (majority).

The new leader runs Phase 1 over the in-flight log slots, learns of any partially-committed values, and runs Phase 2 to complete them.

The old leader on the minority side is "isolated": it cannot commit, cannot get accepts. Its state remains valid (safety is preserved), but it makes no progress. When the network heals and the old leader rejoins, it discovers a higher ballot in use, steps down, and becomes a follower.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
The result: brief unavailability (during the election, typically seconds), then resumed service from the new leader on the majority side. No safety violation; the worst case is the brief pause.

**Q3.** Compare Paxos to a 2-phase commit (2PC). Both have two phases. What is fundamentally different about how they handle coordinator failure?

Hint

2PC has one coordinator; if it crashes, participants block. Paxos has multiple proposers; if one crashes, another can take over.

**Answer:** Both protocols have two phases. The structural difference is in how each handles the failure of the coordinator/proposer.

_2PC structure_ : one coordinator sends PREPARE (or VOTE_REQUEST) to all participants. If all participants vote yes, the coordinator sends COMMIT. If any vote no, the coordinator sends ABORT. The coordinator is the single decision-maker.

_2PC failure_ : if the coordinator crashes after PREPARE but before sending COMMIT/ABORT, participants are blocked. They have voted yes (and hold locks) but do not know the coordinator's decision. They cannot decide unilaterally because the coordinator might have committed (informed downstream clients) before crashing.

_Paxos structure_ : any proposer can propose. The protocol's safety holds even if multiple proposers run concurrently. A new proposer can take over by picking a higher ballot number.

_Paxos failure_ : if a proposer crashes mid-protocol, another proposer can take over by picking a higher ballot. The new proposer's Phase 1 learns what (if anything) was accepted, and either completes the previous proposal or starts fresh. No participant is blocked indefinitely.

The structural advantage: Paxos has no single point of failure for liveness. Any process can be the proposer; failure of any single process does not block the system (provided a majority survives).

2PC's blocking failure mode is why it is not used as a general consensus primitive. Practical 2PC implementations replicate the coordinator state via Paxos (or Raft), so the coordinator's state is recoverable after coordinator failure. This is the Spanner pattern (Chapter 13): 2PC for the cross-shard transaction, Paxos within each shard for the per-shard durability.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "In 2026, Paxos is obsolete. Raft is just as good, simpler, and what every new system should use."

**Discussion:** Defense: Raft was explicitly designed by Ongaro and Ousterhout — as described in their 2014 paper "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm" — to be more understandable than Paxos while providing the same safety guarantees. Most new distributed systems (etcd, Consul, TiKV, CockroachDB, SpiceDB) use Raft. Diego Ongaro's thesis ("Designing for Understandability") explicitly targets Paxos's complexity. From a fresh-team perspective, Raft is the right default.

Refutation: Paxos has properties that Raft does not, depending on the variant. EPaxos (Egalitarian Paxos) is leaderless; for workloads with very low contention, it has higher throughput than Raft's leader-bottleneck design. Flexible Paxos lets the operator tune the quorum sizes, which Raft does not. Google's Chubby and Spanner are Paxos-based and have decades of production scar tissue baked in.

The synthesis: for new general-purpose systems, Raft is the right choice in 2026. The implementation cost is lower; the operational ergonomics are better. For specialized systems (very low contention, very high throughput, unusual fault models), Paxos variants may still be worth the implementation complexity. The "Paxos vs Raft" debate is largely settled in favor of Raft for the common case, with Paxos surviving in the niches where its variants give real advantages.

A second consideration: ZooKeeper's ZAB (atomic broadcast) is a Paxos variant, and a large fraction of production infrastructure depends on ZooKeeper. So Paxos is operationally alive even in systems that do not advertise themselves as "using Paxos." The protocol family is more present than naive name-matching suggests.

**Q2.** An LLM is asked to implement Paxos in Python and produces 200 lines of code. Without running it, identify three classes of bugs that are likely to be in any LLM-generated Paxos implementation.

**Discussion:**

(a) **Persistence omissions.** Acceptor state (bmaxb_{max}bmax​, accepted_ballot, accepted_value) must be persisted _before_ responding to prepare or accept messages. LLM-generated code often uses in-memory state with no fsync, no WAL, no recovery. After a crash, the acceptor "forgets" prior promises and can accept conflicting values, violating safety. This is invisible in single-process testing.

(b) **Ballot uniqueness.** Ballot numbers must be unique across all proposers and monotonically increasing per-proposer. LLM code often uses a simple counter without proposer-ID disambiguation, so two proposers can use the same ballot, breaking the protocol's "highest accepted ballot" tie-breaking.

(c) **Quorum off-by-one.** The majority of NNN is ⌈(N+1)/2⌉\lceil (N+1)/2 \rceil⌈(N+1)/2⌉. For N=4N=4N=4, majority is 3; for N=5N=5N=5, majority is 3. LLM code often hardcodes the wrong value, breaking quorum intersection when used with an even number of nodes.

Three more (any of which causes silent safety violations):

(d) **Phase 2 value selection.** The accept rule (proposer must propose the highest-accepted-ballot value from Phase 1 responses) is the central safety invariant. LLM code often uses its own value unconditionally, which violates safety the moment a proposer crashes mid-protocol.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 8: Paxos — The Original
blocks.src:
(e) **Reconfiguration.** Adding or removing nodes requires careful protocol-level coordination. LLM-generated code typically does not implement reconfiguration at all, or does so naively in a way that allows split-brain.

(f) **Network framing.** Paxos messages must be reliably matched to the correct proposer/ballot/acceptor. LLM code often uses simple HTTP without idempotency, so retried messages can be processed twice, corrupting acceptor state.

The deeper observation: Paxos is the worst-case category for LLM-generated code. The safety properties are not visible in any single test run; they require adversarial scheduling (failures at specific moments) to reveal. An LLM that has been trained on Paxos descriptions but not on Paxos implementations will produce code that looks right and is silently unsafe. This is the central lesson of Chapter 27: distributed code requires reasoning that LLMs do not currently do well.


### Chapter Summary

Paxos is the canonical consensus protocol, introduced by Lamport in 1989. Single-decree Paxos agrees on one value via two phases (prepare, accept) plus quorum intersection. The safety property is preserved by the rule that any proposer's accept must propose the highest-accepted value from prepare responses; this ensures once a value is chosen, all subsequent ballots will propose it.

Multi-Paxos extends single-decree to a sequence by electing a stable leader and amortizing Phase 1 over many decisions. The per-decision cost in steady state is one round-trip.

Paxos is notoriously hard to implement: persistence discipline, ballot uniqueness, quorum off-by-one, reconfiguration, snapshotting. Spanner and Megastore are the canonical production implementations. The reading list in Appendix A includes the original 1998 paper, the 2001 "Paxos Made Simple" rewrite, and Lampson's "How to Build a Highly Available System Using Consensus" for the operational view.

Chapter 9 takes Raft, which Ongaro and Ousterhout designed in 2014 to be more understandable than Paxos. Raft uses the same skeleton (quorum + leader + persistent state) but in a form that is easier to teach, easier to implement, and easier to reason about operationally. It is the consensus protocol of choice for new systems in 2026.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
Anya Reddy joined Stratus DB two months ago. Her first project: pick a consensus library for the replication layer. She read the Paxos papers. She read the Megastore paper. She tried to implement single-decree Paxos in a weekend. She came in Monday morning and said: "I can't keep all of this in my head. There must be a better way."

Her tech lead handed her the Raft paper.

Raft, designed by Ongaro and Ousterhout and published in their 2014 paper "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm," was built with a specific goal: be at least as correct as Paxos, but be _understandable_. The abstract explicitly frames understandability as the primary contribution.

This chapter teaches Raft as Anya learned it: the three sub-problems (leader election, log replication, safety), the role of terms, the AppendEntries protocol, and why every new distributed-systems project in 2026 reaches for Raft first.


### 9.1 The Three Sub-Problems

Raft decomposes consensus into three orthogonal pieces:

(a) **Leader election** : choose one server to be the leader. (b) **Log replication** : the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log, and replicates them to followers. (c) **Safety** : ensure that once a log entry is committed, it stays committed and no other server commits a conflicting entry at the same index.

The decomposition matters pedagogically: each piece can be understood (and tested) independently. Paxos's monolithic structure makes this harder; Raft's split is the central design decision.


### 9.2 Terms

Time in Raft is divided into _terms_. Each term has at most one leader. Terms are numbered with monotonically increasing integers. Every RPC message in Raft carries the sender's current term.

The term is Raft's analog of Paxos's ballot number. The rules:

* Each server stores `currentTerm` (its highest known term) on stable storage.
* Whenever a server sees a higher term in any RPC, it updates its own `currentTerm` and reverts to follower (if it was a leader or candidate).
* A server that sees a lower term in an RPC rejects the RPC with the higher current term in the response.

The "always defer to a higher term" rule prevents stale leaders from making decisions. An old leader that has been deposed but does not yet know it (perhaps it was paused or partitioned) discovers its outdated status as soon as it tries to communicate with any node that has seen the new term.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
### 9.3 Leader Election

Each server starts as a _follower_. A follower expects regular heartbeats from a leader. If a follower goes too long without a heartbeat (the _election timeout_ , typically randomized between 150 ms and 300 ms), it becomes a _candidate_.

A candidate:

  1. Increments its `currentTerm`.
  2. Votes for itself.
  3. Resets its election timer.
  4. Sends `RequestVote` RPCs to all other servers.

Each server, upon receiving `RequestVote`:

* If the candidate's term is lower than its own, rejects.
* If it has already voted in this term, rejects (each server votes at most once per term).
* If the candidate's log is at least as up-to-date as its own (more on this below), grants the vote.

A candidate that collects votes from a majority becomes leader. A leader's first action is to send heartbeats (empty `AppendEntries` RPCs) to all followers, asserting its leadership.

If two candidates split the vote (neither wins majority), both wait for the next election timeout and try again. The randomized timeout makes simultaneous re-elections statistically unlikely; after a few rounds, one candidate's timer fires significantly earlier and it wins.


#### The "log up-to-date" rule

A candidate's log is considered "up-to-date" if either:

(a) The candidate's last log entry has a higher term than the voter's last entry, or (b) Both have the same last-entry term, and the candidate's log is at least as long.

This rule ensures that the elected leader has all committed entries. If a candidate were elected with a shorter log than some committed entry, that entry could be "lost" (the leader would overwrite it). The up-to-date rule prevents this.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
### 9.4 Log Replication — Workflow 4: Raft State-Machine Walkthrough

> **Workflow 4 (input → output)** : given a stream of client requests and an N-node Raft cluster, produce a replicated state machine where every committed entry survives any minority failure and every client request is applied exactly once (in the same order) on every replica. The mechanism is Raft's leader-election + AppendEntries + commit-on-majority. Variations: per-range Raft (CockroachDB) for horizontal scale; multi-Raft (TiKV) for many groups in parallel; learner nodes for catchup without affecting quorum. The skill being trained: implement (or operate) a system that maintains the safety property "committed entry at index i in term T stays at index i forever" through arbitrary leader changes and partitions.

The leader accepts client requests. For each request:

  1. Append the entry to its local log.
  2. Send `AppendEntries` RPCs to all followers in parallel, containing the new entry plus context (previous log index and term).
  3. Once a majority of followers have replicated the entry, mark it as _committed_ and apply it to the state machine.
  4. Respond to the client.

The followers' `AppendEntries` handling:

* If the leader's term is lower than the follower's, reject.
* If the follower's log does not contain an entry at the previous-index with the previous-term, reject. This is the _consistency check_ ; it ensures the follower's log matches the leader's log up to that point.
* Otherwise, append the new entries (overwriting any conflicting ones), update the commit index, and respond success.

The consistency check is the heart of Raft's safety. By requiring the follower's log to match the leader's up to the point of the new append, Raft ensures the log grows as an _append-only_ , _consistent_ sequence across all replicas.


#### What happens when a follower's log is behind

If the follower's log does not contain the previous-index entry (it is too short), or contains a different entry (the term mismatches), the follower rejects. The leader, on rejection, decrements its `nextIndex` for that follower and retries with the earlier entry. This continues until the leader finds a point where the follower's log matches, then appends all subsequent entries.

The bookkeeping: the leader maintains `nextIndex[follower]` (the next entry to send) and `matchIndex[follower]` (the highest entry known to be replicated on that follower). After a successful append, both advance.


### 9.5 Safety

Raft's safety property: if a leader has committed an entry at index iii in term TTT, no other leader in any future term will ever commit a different entry at index iii.

The argument depends on three rules already stated:

(a) Each term has at most one leader (election majority). (b) Each new leader has all committed entries (election restriction via the "log up-to-date" rule). (c) Leaders never overwrite or delete their log entries.

Together: a committed entry at index iii in term TTT is replicated on a majority by the time it is committed. Any future leader must have been elected by a majority. The two majorities intersect (quorum intersection); the intersection node has the entry. By the up-to-date rule, the new leader must have at least all entries that any majority-member has, which includes the committed entry. So the new leader has it, and it remains at index iii forever.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
#### The "leader can only commit entries from its own term" subtlety

A subtle rule: a leader does _not_ commit entries from previous terms directly by replicating them. It commits a previous-term entry only by replicating an entry from its own term (which has the side effect of committing the previous entries as well).

Why: without this rule, a corner case allows a committed entry to be later overwritten. The Raft paper's Figure 8 illustrates the case; the fix is the "current term only" commit rule. This is the one subtle safety condition in Raft; without it, the protocol is unsafe.


#### Common Misconception

A common misreading of Raft: "the leader replicates and as soon as a majority ack, it's committed." Almost right, but with the previous-term-commit subtlety. The leader commits an entry by ensuring (a) a majority have replicated it and (b) an entry from the current term has also been replicated to a majority. The two conditions together prevent the Figure 8 issue.

In practice, this rarely matters because new leaders typically commit fresh entries quickly, but implementations must handle the corner case.


### 9.6 Log Compaction

Raft logs grow without bound. Production systems use snapshotting: periodically, the state machine's full state is written to a snapshot, and the log is truncated to the snapshot's index.

The snapshot includes:

* The full state machine state (e.g., the key-value store contents).
* The last index and term included in the snapshot.
* The current cluster configuration.

A follower whose log is too far behind to catch up via `AppendEntries` receives a snapshot via `InstallSnapshot` RPC. The follower replaces its state with the snapshot and resumes.

The operational consideration: snapshots must be consistent with the state machine. Many implementations have a bug where the snapshot is taken at one moment, but log entries committed during snapshot creation are not properly accounted for. The fix is careful coordination between the snapshot routine and the apply routine.


### 9.7 Cluster Membership Changes

Adding or removing servers from the Raft cluster is itself a configuration change that must go through consensus. The naive approach (suddenly change the configuration) is unsafe: two different "majorities" can briefly exist (one majority of the old configuration, one majority of the new), and they can elect different leaders.

Raft's solution: _joint consensus_. The transition from configuration ColdC_{old}Cold​ to CnewC_{new}Cnew​ goes through an intermediate configuration Cold,newC_{old,new}Cold,new​ that requires majorities of _both_ old and new. During the transition, any decision needs joint majority. After the transition, the cluster switches to CnewC_{new}Cnew​ only.

This is one of the more complex parts of Raft and is often the source of implementation bugs. Simpler alternatives (single-server change at a time) are used in production etcd; the trade-off is more steps for the same logical change.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
### 9.8 Why Raft Won

In 2026, Raft is the consensus choice for almost every new distributed system. Why:

* **Pedagogical clarity** : the three sub-problems are independent; engineers can learn one at a time.
* **Implementation-friendly** : explicit log structure, explicit role transitions, explicit state machine API.
* **Mature ecosystem** : etcd's Raft implementation (Go) is widely used; many language-specific implementations exist.
* **Operational tooling** : etcdctl, consul members, CockroachDB's raft visualizer. The protocol exposes enough state to be observable.
* **Community knowledge** : a generation of engineers learned Raft as their first consensus protocol; the knowledge base is broad.

Production users include: etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, MongoDB (since 3.6), HashiCorp Vault, SpiceDB, NATS JetStream, RethinkDB (historically), and many internal company systems.

Paxos still wins in some niches: Google's infrastructure (Chubby, Spanner), specialized variants like EPaxos for high-throughput leaderless workloads, Flexible Paxos for tunable quorums. But for a fresh project in 2026, the default is Raft.


### 9.9 Anya's Decision

Anya picked the `tikv/raft-rs` library (Rust) for the Stratus DB replication layer. Her reasoning, captured in the design doc:

(a) **Maturity** : TiKV's Raft has been running in production for years, with the bugs found and fixed. (b) **Language fit** : Stratus DB is Rust; raft-rs is native. (c) **Operational tooling** : the library exposes the state machine, log, and configuration in a form Stratus's existing observability stack can ingest. (d) **Membership change** : raft-rs implements single-server changes (the safer subset of Raft's joint consensus).

What she gave up: leaderless writes (which CRDTs or EPaxos could give); per-tablet performance tuning (which Spanner's Paxos-with-leases gives). For Stratus's use case (financial-grade durability, sub-100ms commits, three-region deployment), these trade-offs are right.

The pattern Anya followed is the 2026 standard: pick a mature Raft library, lean on its tooling, accept the operational defaults until you need to tune. The chapters ahead (Chapters 11-14) show how Stratus and CockroachDB build distributed databases on top of this Raft foundation.


### 9.10 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Raft decomposes consensus into three sub-problems. Name them and state what each handles.

Hint

Leader election, log replication, safety.

**Answer:**

(a) **Leader election** : choose a single server to be the leader. Followers detect leader absence via heartbeat timeout and start elections. The randomized timeout reduces split-vote probability. The "log up-to-date" rule ensures elected leaders have all committed entries.

(b) **Log replication** : the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log, and replicates to followers via `AppendEntries`. An entry is committed once a majority have replicated it. Followers apply committed entries to their state machine.

(c) **Safety** : ensure that once an entry is committed at a given index, no future leader will commit a different entry at the same index. The mechanism is the combination of election restriction (only candidates with up-to-date logs can win) and the leader's append-only log discipline.

**Q2.** What is a Raft "term" and how does it differ from a Paxos ballot?

Hint

Term is monotonically increasing; one leader per term; serves the same role as Paxos ballot.

**Answer:** A Raft term is a monotonically increasing integer that divides time. Each term begins with an election; at most one leader is elected per term. Every Raft RPC carries the sender's term, and any node seeing a higher term updates its own and reverts to follower.

Compared to Paxos ballots:

* Paxos ballot numbers are also monotonically increasing and total-ordered. The structural role (preventing stale proposals from being accepted) is similar.
* Paxos ballots can be created freely by any proposer at any time. Raft terms are created only by candidates starting elections, which makes Raft's term sequence more orderly.
* Paxos has no concept of "term" leader; Multi-Paxos has a leader, but the leader's role is not as tightly coupled to the ballot as Raft's leader is to the term.

The conceptual mapping: a Raft term corresponds to a Multi-Paxos "leader's tenure during which it runs a single Phase 1." The differences are mostly notational and ergonomic.

**Q3.** Why does Raft randomize the election timeout?

Hint

To reduce split votes when multiple followers' timers fire simultaneously.

**Answer:** If election timeouts were fixed at, say, 200 ms, all followers in a cluster would tend to fire their timers at roughly the same moment after a leader fails. Multiple followers would become candidates simultaneously, request votes simultaneously, and split the vote (none gets a majority). The cluster would re-attempt the election, and likely split again.

Randomizing the timeout (e.g., uniform random between 150 ms and 300 ms) makes simultaneous candidates statistically unlikely. After a few rounds, one follower's timer fires significantly earlier, and that follower wins the election before the others' timers fire.

The randomization is a small but important practical detail. Without it, Raft's leader election would frequently livelock under crash conditions. With it, leader election completes in expected time on the order of the maximum timeout (a few hundred milliseconds in production).

**Q4.** Describe the AppendEntries consistency check. What does it guarantee?

Hint

The follower must have the previous entry matching the leader's record before appending the new one.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
**Answer:** When the leader sends `AppendEntries(term, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries, leaderCommit)`, the follower performs the consistency check:

(a) If `term < currentTerm`, reject (the leader is stale).

(b) If the follower's log does not contain an entry at `prevLogIndex`, reject (the follower is too short).

(c) If the follower's log entry at `prevLogIndex` does not have term `prevLogTerm`, reject (the follower's log has diverged from the leader's at this point).

Otherwise, append the new entries (overwriting any conflicting subsequent entries), advance the commit index per `leaderCommit`, and reply success.

What this guarantees: after a successful `AppendEntries`, the follower's log matches the leader's log up to the new entries' end. The log structures across the cluster are kept consistent by this incremental check.

When the consistency check rejects, the leader decrements `nextIndex[follower]` and retries with an earlier entry. The leader and follower converge to a matching log prefix, then append all subsequent entries.

This protocol is the mechanism by which a lagging or partition-recovered follower catches up to the leader's log.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Anya is implementing the Stratus DB replication layer. She has a 3-node Raft cluster. A follower has been partitioned from the cluster for 30 minutes; during that time, the cluster committed 1000 entries. The follower rejoins. Walk through how it catches up.

Hint

The leader detects the follower is behind via repeated AppendEntries rejections. It walks back nextIndex until it finds a match, then forward-appends. For very large gaps, InstallSnapshot may be used.

**Answer:** When the follower rejoins:

(a) The leader's next heartbeat (`AppendEntries` with `entries=[]`) reaches the follower. The leader's `nextIndex[follower]` is still pointing at the entry the leader was tracking before the partition.

(b) The follower's log lacks the entry at `prevLogIndex` (it is 1000 entries behind). The follower rejects.

(c) The leader receives the rejection. It decrements `nextIndex[follower]` and retries. This continues until `nextIndex` points at an entry the follower has.

For an efficient implementation, the rejection response includes the follower's last log index, so the leader can jump `nextIndex` to that value rather than decrementing one at a time.

(d) Once a match is found, the leader sends the next batch of entries (typically batched, dozens or hundreds at a time). The follower appends, advances its commit index per the leader's `leaderCommit`, and replies success.

(e) Batch by batch, the follower catches up to the current log end. With 1000 entries and a 50ms RTT, batching 100 entries per RPC, the catchup takes about 500 ms of network time plus disk write time on the follower.

If the gap is very large (e.g., the log has been truncated past the follower's last entry due to snapshotting), the leader sends an `InstallSnapshot` RPC. The follower replaces its state with the snapshot and resumes normal `AppendEntries`-based replication from the snapshot's end.

In production etcd / TiKV / Raft-based systems, this catchup is typically transparent and finishes within seconds for gaps of thousands of entries.

**Q2.** A Raft cluster has 5 nodes. During a network partition, 2 nodes are isolated from the other 3. Walk through what happens to each side and what the user-visible behavior is.

Hint

The majority side (3) can elect a leader and commit; the minority side (2) cannot.

**Answer:** During the partition:

_Majority side (3 nodes):_

(a) If the previous leader was on the majority side, it continues operating. Its heartbeats reach 2 of 3 nodes; it has majority for AppendEntries. Commits proceed normally.

(b) If the previous leader was on the minority side, the majority-side followers' timers fire (no heartbeats received). One becomes candidate, gets votes from 2 of 3 (majority), becomes leader. New commits proceed.

(c) Either way, the majority side continues serving writes and linearizable reads.

_Minority side (2 nodes):_

(a) If the previous leader is on the minority side, it tries to commit but cannot get majority (it has only itself plus possibly one other reachable node; total 2 of 5 needed 3). Writes block.

(b) If the previous leader was on the majority side, the minority-side followers wait for heartbeats. Their timers fire. One becomes candidate, requests votes from the other minority node. It gets 2 votes (self + other), but 2 < 3, so it does not become leader. Re-election fails repeatedly.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
(c) The minority side cannot serve writes. It can serve stale reads (the last-known committed entries) if the application accepts staleness; otherwise, reads also fail.

_User-visible:_

* Clients connected to the majority side: normal operation, no awareness of the partition.
* Clients connected to the minority side: writes fail with "no leader" or timeout; reads fail or return stale data.

_Recovery:_

* When the partition heals, the minority side's nodes discover the higher term in the majority side's heartbeats. They revert to follower, sync their logs to the majority's, and rejoin.
* No data loss; no inconsistency. The minority's pending writes were never committed and are abandoned.

**Q3.** Compare Raft's leader-based design to a leaderless approach (e.g., EPaxos, Cassandra LWT). What does Raft give up by having a single leader, and what does it gain?

Hint

Single leader is a bottleneck and a single point of failure for liveness; in exchange, the protocol is simpler and serializes ordering trivially.

**Answer:** Raft's leader-based design has a single leader at any time. All client requests go through the leader; followers replicate.

_What Raft gives up:_

(a) **Throughput ceiling**. The leader serializes all commits, so per-cluster throughput is bounded by the leader's processing capacity and the network bandwidth to followers. Sharding (multi-raft per range, as in CockroachDB) is the way around this.

(b) **Leader as bottleneck**. A slow or overloaded leader slows the entire cluster. Operators tune leader placement to avoid hot-spot issues.

(c) **Failover unavailability**. When a leader dies, the cluster pauses for an election (typically seconds). Leaderless protocols have no such window.

(d) **Geographic asymmetry**. A leader in one region means all writes pay round-trip to that region; clients in other regions see higher write latency. Leaderless protocols can let any region accept writes.

_What Raft gains:_

(a) **Simplicity**. Single leader serializes all writes; ordering is trivial. The protocol is much simpler than leaderless alternatives.

(b) **Implementation maturity**. Many production-quality Raft libraries exist; few leaderless equivalents.

(c) **Predictable performance**. The leader's behavior is predictable; latency and throughput characteristics are well-understood.

(d) **Operational tooling**. Almost all Raft-based systems have visibility tools (etcd's status, CockroachDB's raft inspector); leaderless protocols often lack similar tooling.

The trade-off: leader-based Raft is the right default for systems where simplicity and operational maturity outweigh the latency floor of leader-routing. Leaderless protocols win for very-high-throughput workloads where the leader bottleneck dominates, or for geo-distributed workloads where any-region-writes are required.

In 2026, the dominant pattern is multi-Raft: many Raft groups in parallel, each handling a shard. This combines Raft's per-group simplicity with horizontal scale-out. CockroachDB, TiKV, and YugabyteDB all use this pattern.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "Raft's simplicity is a marketing claim; once you implement reconfiguration, snapshotting, and joint consensus, Raft is just as complex as Paxos."

**Discussion:** Defense: the core Raft protocol (leader election + AppendEntries + commit) is genuinely simpler than core Paxos (prepare + accept + multi-paxos optimization). A student can implement a working basic Raft in a weekend; basic Paxos takes longer. The pedagogical and code-readability gains are real.

Refutation: the full Raft implementation, including reconfiguration via joint consensus, snapshotting, leadership transfer, leader-step-down, pre-vote, learner nodes (for catchup without affecting quorum), and the various optimizations, is comparable in complexity to a full Multi-Paxos implementation. Diego Ongaro's PhD thesis is hundreds of pages; the etcd Raft implementation is thousands of lines.

The synthesis: Raft is simpler in the _base case_ and the _common case_. The full feature set is comparable in complexity to full Paxos. But: the base-case simplicity matters because (a) most users do not need the full feature set, (b) understanding the base case is the prerequisite for understanding the full set, and (c) operational reasoning about Raft's behavior is easier because the base case is so clear.

A more honest claim: "Raft is simpler for the 80% of users who need the base case, and at parity with Paxos for the 20% who need the full feature set." This is sufficient to make Raft the right default for new systems.

**Q2.** An LLM is asked to "implement Raft for a distributed counter." The output is 300 lines of Python. Identify three structural bugs likely to be present in any LLM-generated Raft implementation, beyond the Paxos-equivalent bugs from Chapter 8.

**Discussion:** Beyond the persistence, ballot uniqueness, and quorum off-by-one bugs of Chapter 8:

(a) **Term-restart of vote count.** The vote-collection state must be cleared at the start of each new term. If the LLM caches vote counts across terms or fails to reset on term increase, the candidate may count stale votes.

(b) **Apply-on-leader-only confusion.** Entries are committed when a majority replicate; they are _applied_ to the state machine after commit. Many LLM implementations apply on append rather than on commit, which causes uncommitted entries to be visible in the state machine and breaks safety on leader failure.

(c) **Previous-term-commit subtlety.** Raft's rule that a leader commits previous-term entries only by also committing a current-term entry is subtle. LLM implementations frequently miss this and commit previous-term entries directly, which violates safety in the Figure 8 corner case.

Three more (any of which causes silent safety violations):

(d) **AppendEntries consistency check off-by-one.** The check compares the follower's entry at `prevLogIndex` to `prevLogTerm`. Off-by-one in either index or term comparison causes inconsistent logs to remain inconsistent.

(e) **NextIndex back-tracking.** When `AppendEntries` is rejected, the leader must decrement `nextIndex` and retry. LLM implementations sometimes fail to decrement, causing infinite-loop retries that look like a hang.

(f) **Snapshotting race with apply.** The snapshot captures the state-machine state at some moment; concurrent apply must not modify the state during snapshotting. LLM implementations rarely coordinate this, producing inconsistent snapshots.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 9: Raft — The Implementation-Friendly Alternative
blocks.src:
The pattern, as with Paxos: LLM-generated code matches the high-level description but misses the subtle invariants. The Raft paper's Figure 8 case is in the paper; LLM training has seen it. But translating "the leader must commit a current-term entry to commit previous-term entries" into correct code requires understanding the invariant deeply, which the model does not do.

The safest pattern in 2026: use a vetted Raft library (etcd's raft, raft-rs, hashicorp/raft); do not generate consensus code from scratch via LLM. Use generated code only for the application logic on top of the library.


### Chapter Summary

Raft is the consensus protocol of choice for new distributed systems in 2026. It decomposes consensus into three orthogonal sub-problems (leader election, log replication, safety) and provides a clean operational model based on terms, elections, and the AppendEntries consistency check.

Anya's choice for Stratus DB (use raft-rs, lean on the library's tooling, accept operational defaults) is the 2026 pattern. Most teams should not implement Raft from scratch; the mature libraries handle the edge cases (reconfiguration, snapshotting, leader transfer) that consume most of the implementation effort.

Raft trades a per-cluster throughput ceiling (the leader serializes writes) for simplicity and operational tooling. The multi-Raft pattern (many Raft groups in parallel, one per shard) restores horizontal scale-out. CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB, and others use this pattern in production.

Chapter 10 takes the next step beyond crash-failure consensus: what if some nodes lie? Byzantine fault tolerance (HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Tendermint) extends consensus to adversarial settings. The cost is higher (3f+1 replicas instead of 2f+1), but the threat model covers blockchain, untrusted clouds, and high-stakes financial systems. The chapter also covers Flexible Paxos (Heidi Howard's reconfiguration insight), which lets operators tune the consistency-availability trade-off beyond what fixed-quorum protocols allow.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
Raft assumes nodes only fail by crashing. They stop sending messages; they do not send wrong messages. They do not lie about their log, equivocate (send different messages to different peers), or attempt to deceive the protocol. This assumption is reasonable when the cluster is operated by one trusted team in one trusted environment. It is not reasonable when the cluster's nodes are operated by mutually distrustful parties (blockchain validators), when nodes might be compromised by an attacker (cloud environments with hostile tenants), or when software bugs produce "Byzantine-like" behavior (corrupted state, garbage messages). Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) protocols handle these conditions. The cost: 3f+13f + 13f+1 replicas to tolerate fff Byzantine faults (vs 2f+12f + 12f+1 for crash-only). The benefit: the protocol works correctly even when up to fff nodes actively misbehave. This chapter covers the modern BFT protocols: HotStuff (the basis of every 2026 BFT system), Narwhal-Bullshark (DAG-mempool plus consensus separation), Tendermint (the workhorse BFT for many blockchain ecosystems), Flexible Paxos (Heidi Howard's reconfiguration insight), and the non-blockchain BFT use case (control planes for adversarial multi-tenant systems). Each general has an opinion. Some generals are traitors and may send conflicting messages to different other generals. The loyal generals must agree on an action despite the traitors. In distributed-systems terms: NNN nodes, some of which are _Byzantine_ (may send arbitrary messages, including different messages to different peers). The protocol must guarantee: * All correct nodes decide the same value. * The decided value is valid (depending on validity definition). * The protocol terminates (with the usual partial-synchrony assumption). The classical impossibility: BFT requires N≥3f+1N \ge 3f + 1N≥3f+1 where fff is the maximum number of Byzantine nodes. The additional node breaks the symmetry.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
### 10.2 PBFT: The Classical Protocol

Practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance, introduced by Castro and Liskov in their 1999 paper, was the first BFT protocol practical enough to deploy. PBFT has three phases per decision:

(a) **Pre-prepare** : the leader proposes a value, sends to all replicas. (b) **Prepare** : each replica that accepts the pre-prepare broadcasts a prepare message to all others. A replica that collects 2f+12f + 12f+1 prepare messages enters the "prepared" state for this value. (c) **Commit** : each prepared replica broadcasts a commit message. A replica that collects 2f+12f + 12f+1 commit messages decides the value.

Why two rounds (prepare + commit)? The prepare round ensures that no two correct replicas can simultaneously prepare different values (quorum intersection). The commit round ensures that if any correct replica commits, all correct replicas eventually do (uniformity).

PBFT's complexity: each phase is all-to-all broadcast, giving O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) messages per decision. For N=4N = 4N=4 (tolerating 1 Byzantine), this is 16 messages per decision; manageable. For N=100N = 100N=100, it is 10,000 messages, prohibitive.

PBFT was the canonical BFT protocol for two decades but was rarely deployed at scale due to its quadratic message complexity. The 2018-2020 wave of blockchain research produced descendants that addressed the complexity.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
### 10.3 HotStuff: Linear View Change — Workflow 5: HotStuff Three-Phase Trace

> **Workflow 5 (input → output)** : given an N-validator BFT cluster (N ≥ 3f+1) and a stream of proposals, produce committed decisions despite up to f Byzantine validators, with O(N) view-change cost. The mechanism is HotStuff's three-phase voting (prepare / pre-commit / commit) with Quorum Certificates as compact support proofs, plus pipelining for throughput. Variations: Tendermint for simpler implementation at lower throughput; Narwhal-Bullshark for DAG-based mempool separation; Mysticeti for further throughput optimization. The skill being trained: trace a proposal through three phases; understand why each phase is necessary; reason about what happens to in-flight proposals during a leader change.

HotStuff, introduced by Yin, Malkhi, Reiter, Gueta, and Abraham in their 2019 paper, was the breakthrough that made BFT practical at larger scale. The key innovation: a linear view-change protocol that reduces the message complexity per leader change from O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) to O(N)O(N)O(N).

HotStuff's three-phase structure resembles PBFT but with critical differences:

* Each phase is a _vote round_ : replicas vote on the leader's proposal; the leader collects 2f+12f + 12f+1 votes into a _Quorum Certificate (QC)_.
* The QC is the proof that the value has support; subsequent phases reference the QC by hash, not by re-broadcasting all votes.
* The view-change (when a leader is suspected) is linear because the new leader needs only the QC from the highest committed phase, not all messages from all replicas.

Pipelining: HotStuff pipelines the phases. While the leader is collecting votes for phase 1 of block k+1k+1k+1, it can be collecting phase 2 votes for block kkk and phase 3 votes for block k−1k-1k−1. This makes the throughput much higher than PBFT's straight three-phase serial execution.

HotStuff variants are the basis of every modern BFT system: Diem/Aptos uses HotStuff, Sui uses Bullshark on top of Narwhal (which incorporates HotStuff ideas), Mysticeti (the 2024 high-throughput Sui consensus) extends HotStuff with DAG-based mempool.


#### Common Misconception

A common confusion: "HotStuff is for blockchain only." HotStuff is a _consensus protocol_ ; blockchains use it because their threat model requires BFT, but the protocol itself is applicable to any BFT use case. Non-blockchain HotStuff deployments include high-stakes financial control planes and security-critical configuration stores.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
### 10.4 Narwhal-Bullshark: DAG-Based Consensus

The 2022 Narwhal paper (Danezis, Kokoris-Kogias, Sonnino, Spiegelman) made a structural innovation: separate the _mempool_ (the layer that orders transactions before they reach consensus) from the _consensus_ (the layer that decides which mempool blocks to commit).

The Narwhal mempool is a _Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)_ of mini-blocks, each signed by its producer and referencing prior mini-blocks. The DAG structure means many producers can extend the graph in parallel, without waiting for a leader to order them.

Consensus runs on top of the DAG: a leader's job is no longer "order transactions" (the DAG already orders them) but "pick a frontier of the DAG to commit." This dramatically reduces the work the leader must do.

Bullshark — designed by Spiegelman and colleagues and published in 2022 — is a consensus protocol that runs on top of the Narwhal DAG. It produces commits with low latency by exploiting the DAG's structure: the leader can commit blocks already in the DAG without further communication, because the DAG itself is the "agreement" mechanism (every block is signed and referenced).

In production:

* **Aptos** uses a HotStuff-inspired consensus with a separated mempool.
* **Sui** uses Bullshark on Narwhal — upgraded to Mysticeti in 2024 for higher throughput.
* **Diem** (defunct) used HotStuff directly.

The throughput claims for Narwhal-Bullshark are dramatic: tens of thousands of transactions per second, compared to PBFT's hundreds. The latency claims are competitive (sub-second commits). The complexity is in the DAG mempool's correctness and the integration with the consensus layer.


### 10.5 Tendermint: The Workhorse

Tendermint, described in Buchman's 2016 thesis and extended by Buchman, Kwon, and Milosevic in 2018, is the BFT protocol used by Cosmos and many other blockchain ecosystems. Tendermint trades some HotStuff features for simplicity:

* Two-phase voting (prevote + precommit), each requiring 2f+12f + 12f+1 of 3f+13f + 13f+1 votes.
* Round-based: if a round does not reach decision, the next round starts with a new leader chosen via deterministic rotation.
* Locking: once a validator precommits a value, it is "locked" to that value for future rounds.

Tendermint is simpler to implement and debug than HotStuff. Its throughput is lower (because each round is serial, no pipelining) but adequate for many blockchain use cases. The Cosmos ecosystem (Osmosis, Juno, Akash) all use Tendermint.

Tendermint's lock-and-release mechanism (validators locked to a value but able to unlock on certain conditions) is subtle and has been the source of several historical safety bugs in Tendermint forks. The protocol's correctness is well-established; new implementations should use a vetted library rather than re-implementing.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
### 10.6 Flexible Paxos: Tunable Quorums

Heidi Howard's 2016 paper "Flexible Paxos: Quorum Intersection Revisited" generalized Paxos's quorum requirement. The classical Paxos requires both the prepare quorum (Q1Q_1Q1​) and the accept quorum (Q2Q_2Q2​) to be majorities. Howard's insight: only Q1∩Q2≠∅Q_1 \cap Q_2 \ne \emptysetQ1​∩Q2​=∅ is required for safety.

This means: Q1Q_1Q1​ and Q2Q_2Q2​ can be tuned. As long as any prepare quorum intersects any accept quorum, the safety property holds.

Examples:

* Classic: Q1=Q2=⌈N/2⌉+1Q_1 = Q_2 = \lceil N/2 \rceil + 1Q1​=Q2​=⌈N/2⌉+1. Both majorities.
* Grid quorums: Q1Q_1Q1​ = a row, Q2Q_2Q2​ = a column. NNN is a square; both quorums are N\sqrt{N}N​. Saves bandwidth at the cost of higher latency under failure.
* Smaller accept quorums: Q1Q_1Q1​ larger (rarely run), Q2Q_2Q2​ smaller (every commit). Fast commits in steady state.

The implication: a system that runs Phase 1 rarely (stable leadership) can have a _small_ accept quorum for fast commits, at the cost of a _large_ prepare quorum for the infrequent leader change.

This insight is used in some 2026 distributed-database designs to lower per-commit latency without sacrificing safety. CockroachDB and TiDB have variants of this in their roadmap; FoundationDB has had configurable quorum sizes for years.


### 10.7 Non-Blockchain BFT Use Cases

BFT is not just for blockchains. Three production-relevant use cases:

(a) **Cloud control planes** : a cloud's metadata store (which decides where pods run, which network policies apply) is a high-stakes system. If a single node can be compromised, the attacker can move workloads to attacker-controlled nodes. BFT control planes (rare but emerging) defend against this.

(b) **Cross-organizational data sharing** : when two companies share a database (joint ventures, banking syndicates), neither fully trusts the other. A BFT system where both companies operate validators provides shared truth without either party trusting the other unilaterally.

(c) **Configuration stores under attack** : a system that holds high-stakes configuration (TLS certificates, security policies) and might be targeted by attackers can use BFT to ensure no single compromise produces an incorrect configuration.

The cost-benefit: BFT is 2-3x more expensive (more replicas, more messages, more crypto). For most systems, the threat model does not justify the cost. For the small set where it does, the cost is unavoidable.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
### 10.8 Why This Chapter Matters for the Non-Blockchain Reader

The temptation, reading this chapter, is to say: "I'm not building blockchain; I can skip this." This is shortsighted. Three reasons to know BFT:

(a) **Threat models change.** A system designed five years ago for trusted operators may need to tolerate untrusted operators today (acquisition, joint venture, cloud migration). Knowing BFT options means you can evaluate the transition cost when it happens.

(b) **BFT protocols inform crash-failure design.** Many ideas from BFT (pipelining, DAG-based mempool, linear view change) translate back to crash-failure systems. Modern Raft variants (FlexiRaft) incorporate BFT-inspired optimizations.

(c) **BFT is the operational reality for any system involving blockchain.** Whether you are integrating with Ethereum, building on a Cosmos chain, or evaluating an Aptos-based product, the BFT model determines what the underlying system can do.

The 2026 distributed-systems engineer is expected to read a BFT paper and understand it, not to design BFT systems from scratch. The reading list in Appendix A includes the canonical BFT papers (PBFT, HotStuff, Narwhal, Tendermint).


### 10.9 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is a Byzantine fault, and how does it differ from a crash fault?

Hint

Crash: node stops. Byzantine: node sends arbitrary, possibly malicious, messages.

**Answer:** A _crash fault_ is a fault in which a node stops functioning: it stops sending messages, stops responding to messages, and (in the fail-stop model) does not recover until restarted. Crash faults are the assumption of Paxos and Raft.

A _Byzantine fault_ is a fault in which a node behaves arbitrarily: it may send wrong messages, send conflicting messages to different peers (equivocation), pretend to be honest, or actively try to mislead the protocol. Byzantine faults model both malicious behavior (compromised nodes, adversarial validators) and arbitrary software bugs (corrupted state producing garbled responses).

The difference matters because:

(a) Crash-only protocols (Paxos, Raft) assume a non-responsive node is crashed; in Byzantine settings, the same silence might be deliberate, or the node might be sending messages but lying.

(b) Byzantine protocols require 3f+13f + 13f+1 replicas (vs 2f+12f + 12f+1 for crash-only), reflecting the harder problem.
