(c) Byzantine protocols typically require cryptographic signatures on every message (to prove who said what), adding CPU cost.

In 2026, the practical line: if your operators are trusted and your nodes are reasonably secured, crash-failure assumption is right. If operators are untrusted (blockchain validators, joint ventures) or the attack surface includes the nodes themselves, BFT is needed.

**Q2.** Why does BFT require 3f+13f + 13f+1 replicas to tolerate fff Byzantine faults? Sketch the intuition.

Hint

The protocol must distinguish "f Byzantine nodes lying about one node" from "one Byzantine node and f-1 honest nodes giving a different story." The extra node breaks the tie.

**Answer:** Intuition: suppose we have N=3fN = 3fN=3f replicas. The protocol must work correctly when up to fff are Byzantine.

A correct replica receives messages from the others. To form a decision, it needs to identify which messages are from honest peers and which are from Byzantine peers. It cannot tell directly (Byzantine peers can claim anything).

Consider a scenario: fff Byzantine peers all claim "value A is correct." fff honest peers claim "value B is correct." The remaining fff honest peers see this conflict and must decide. From their view: fff say A, fff say B. They cannot distinguish which group is the Byzantine one.

With N=3f+1N = 3f + 1N=3f+1 replicas: any quorum of 2f+12f + 12f+1 contains at least f+1f + 1f+1 honest peers. A quorum of 2f+12f + 12f+1 gives "more than fff honest agreement," which outvotes any Byzantine group of size fff. Two such quorums intersect in at least f+1f + 1f+1 replicas, of which at least 1 is honest, ensuring any two quorum-validated decisions overlap on an honest witness.

This is why BFT needs the additional replica: to give the protocol enough redundancy that any quorum's vote is dominated by honest peers.

**Q3.** What is HotStuff's key innovation over PBFT?

Hint

Linear view change. Quorum certificates that summarize support without rebroadcasting.

**Answer:** HotStuff's key innovation is the _linear view change_ : when a leader is suspected and a new leader takes over, the message complexity is O(N)O(N)O(N) instead of PBFT's O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2).

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
The mechanism: HotStuff uses _Quorum Certificates (QCs)_. A QC is a collection of 2f+12f + 12f+1 signatures on a specific phase's outcome. The QC is a compact, transferable proof of "this value has support."

When the leader collects 2f+12f + 12f+1 votes for phase kkk of a proposal, it forms a QC and broadcasts it (or, in pipelined HotStuff, it includes the QC in the next phase's pre-prepare). The new leader, on a view change, needs only the highest QC from each replica (O(N)O(N)O(N) messages) to determine the protocol's state.

By contrast, PBFT's view change requires every replica to send its full state (the messages it has seen) to the new leader, giving O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) messages.

The implication: HotStuff scales to much larger replica sets (hundreds of validators in some blockchain deployments) without the view-change cost dominating. Pipelining (overlapping the three phases for different proposals) further increases throughput.

**Q4.** Heidi Howard's Flexible Paxos generalizes the quorum requirement. State the generalization and give one example of how it can be used in practice.

Hint

Only Q1 ∩ Q2 ≠ ∅ is required; both don't have to be majorities. Smaller Q2 = faster commits.

**Answer:** Classical Paxos requires the prepare quorum Q1Q_1Q1​ and the accept quorum Q2Q_2Q2​ to each be a majority of NNN replicas. This ensures Q1∩Q2≠∅Q_1 \cap Q_2 \ne \emptysetQ1​∩Q2​=∅ (any two majorities intersect) for safety.

Howard's generalization: only Q1∩Q2≠∅Q_1 \cap Q_2 \ne \emptysetQ1​∩Q2​=∅ is required. The two quorums can be different sizes as long as they intersect.

Practical example: a system with stable leadership runs Phase 1 (prepare) infrequently (e.g., once per leader tenure) and Phase 2 (accept) frequently (every commit). Make Q1Q_1Q1​ large (say, N−1N - 1N−1) and Q2Q_2Q2​ small (say, 2). Any prepare quorum of N−1N - 1N−1 replicas intersects any accept quorum of 2 (because N−1+2>NN - 1 + 2 > NN−1+2>N).

The cost: leader change is expensive (needs N−1N - 1N−1 replicas reachable for prepare). The benefit: every commit needs only 2 replicas to ack, giving very low commit latency in steady state.

For a 5-node cluster: Q1=4Q_1 = 4Q1​=4, Q2=2Q_2 = 2Q2​=2. Commits ack on the leader + 1 other (2 total), much faster than the classical 3-of-5 quorum. Leader changes need 4 of 5 (rare events).

FoundationDB and some newer systems use variants of this for production tuning. The trade-off is a slower-but-rare path for the faster-but-frequent path.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A startup is building a permissioned blockchain for inter-bank settlement. 21 banks will each run a validator node. The threat model: any single bank might be compromised, but no more than 6 simultaneously. Choose between PBFT, HotStuff, and Tendermint, and justify.

Hint

N = 21, f = 6. Check the 3f+1 requirement. Then compare message complexity, throughput, and ecosystem maturity.

**Answer:** Threshold check: 3f+1=19≤N=213f + 1 = 19 \le N = 213f+1=19≤N=21. All three protocols can tolerate 6 Byzantine faults with 21 replicas.

(a) **PBFT** : well-understood, mature. Message complexity O(N2)=441O(N^2) = 441O(N2)=441 messages per decision plus O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) for view change. For 21 nodes, this is workable but limits throughput as the protocol matures. Operational tooling is dated (most PBFT implementations are research code).

(b) **HotStuff** : O(N)O(N)O(N) view change; pipelining allows higher throughput. Adopted by Diem/Aptos in production. Implementation libraries (LibraBFT, Aptos's HotStuff) exist but are tied to specific blockchain ecosystems. Implementing HotStuff for a permissioned chain requires more engineering than picking up a library.

(c) **Tendermint** : simplest of the three. Well-supported via the Cosmos SDK; the Cosmos ecosystem has dozens of production chains. Tendermint Core is a mature, vetted library. Throughput is lower than HotStuff but sufficient for inter-bank settlement (a few hundred TPS, not the thousands HotStuff can do).

Recommendation: Tendermint, via the Cosmos SDK. Reasons:

* Mature library and ecosystem.
* Sufficient throughput for the use case.
* Operational tooling and observability are well-developed.
* The Cosmos IBC (Inter-Blockchain Communication) is a bonus if the chain ever needs to interoperate.

HotStuff is the "best in class" technically but the implementation burden is higher; for a 21-node permissioned chain, Tendermint's simplicity dominates.

PBFT is the wrong choice in 2026: the throughput limitations and outdated tooling make it inferior to either alternative for new deployments.

**Q2.** A cloud provider is designing a metadata store for its control plane. The store must remain correct even if one of the cloud's own data centers is fully compromised. The team is considering BFT. What replication factor do they need, and what are the operational implications?

Hint

"One DC fully compromised" means f = number of validators in that DC. Total N must be ≥ 3f + 1.

**Answer:** If the threat model is "one DC fully compromised," then fff = number of validators in that DC. The total replication factor must be N≥3f+1N \ge 3f + 1N≥3f+1.

If each DC hosts 3 validators (typical for high availability within a DC), then f=3f = 3f=3 and N≥10N \ge 10N≥10. Distributed across 4 DCs (one of which might be compromised), each DC contributes 3 nodes; total 12. N=12≥3⋅3+1=10N = 12 \ge 3 \cdot 3 + 1 = 10N=12≥3⋅3+1=10, satisfied.

Operational implications:

(a) **4 DCs** : the system must span at least 4 DCs to tolerate the loss of one. This is a strong geographic requirement.

(b) **Cross-DC latency** : BFT protocols typically require multiple round-trips per decision. Cross-DC latency (50-200 ms) means each decision is 100-600 ms. The metadata store's per-operation latency is bounded by this.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
(c) **Cryptographic overhead** : signatures on every message; verification cost. For a metadata store at moderate throughput (hundreds of operations per second), the CPU cost is bearable.

(d) **Membership management** : adding or removing validators must itself be done via BFT, since a Byzantine attacker could otherwise introduce extra validators.

(e) **Operational complexity** : 12 validators across 4 DCs means 12 servers to operate, 4 networks to manage, 4 incident-response teams to coordinate. The operational footprint is 3-4x that of a single-region Raft setup.

Trade-off: is "one DC compromised" a realistic threat? For a major cloud provider's control plane, possibly yes (insider threat, targeted attack). For most other systems, the cost of BFT outweighs the probability of the threat. The metadata stores of AWS, GCP, Azure use crash-failure consensus (with strong physical security and access controls) rather than BFT. The threat is real but is managed by other means (defense in depth, monitoring, access control).

**Q3.** Compare HotStuff's pipelining to Raft's log replication. Both can have multiple "decisions in flight" — what is structurally different?

Hint

Raft's leader serializes commits; multiple entries can be in flight but each is independently sent. HotStuff's pipeline overlaps the three voting phases for different proposals.

**Answer:** Both protocols support multiple in-flight decisions, but the structure differs.

_Raft pipelining_ : the leader can send `AppendEntries` for many log entries in parallel. Each entry needs majority acks to commit. The leader can have many entries pending without waiting for each to commit before starting the next. The pipeline is "entries in flight on the network," and each entry has a single round-trip from leader to followers and back.

_HotStuff pipelining_ : HotStuff has three voting phases (prepare, pre-commit, commit) for each decision. The pipeline overlaps these phases for different proposals. While the leader is collecting prepare votes for block k+2k+2k+2, it can be collecting pre-commit votes for block k+1k+1k+1 and commit votes for block kkk. The pipeline is "phases of decisions overlapping," and each decision pays three rounds total but the throughput is one decision per round (rather than one per three rounds).

The structural difference:

* Raft: O(1)O(1)O(1) phases per decision; pipelining is "many decisions at the same phase."
* HotStuff: O(1)O(1)O(1) phases per decision (specifically 3); pipelining is "many decisions at different phases simultaneously."

The throughput effect: Raft can commit one decision per round-trip in steady state. HotStuff can also commit one decision per round-trip in steady state (the pipeline absorbs the three-phase cost). Both have similar peak throughput; the difference shows up in latency (each Raft commit is one round-trip; each HotStuff commit is three round-trips, but they are pipelined so the throughput is the same).

The blockchain implication: HotStuff's per-decision latency is 3 round-trips, which is hundreds of milliseconds to seconds in geo-distributed validator sets. For applications where the per-decision latency matters, this is a cost. For applications where the throughput is what matters (e.g., a blockchain processing many transactions per block), the pipelining absorbs the cost.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "By 2030, all distributed databases should use HotStuff-style BFT, because the threat model includes compromised cloud providers."

**Discussion:** Defense: cloud-provider compromise is a real and growing threat. The Snowden disclosures, the SolarWinds attack, and various nation-state actions demonstrate that "the cloud is trustworthy" is not a safe assumption for high-stakes data. BFT defends against precisely this threat model.

Refutation: the operational cost of BFT (3x replicas, cryptographic overhead, geo-distributed deployment, mature operations) is substantial. For 99% of databases (e-commerce, SaaS, internal tooling), the threat of cloud-provider compromise is hypothetical and the cost is real. Most databases will continue to use crash-failure consensus.

The synthesis: BFT will spread to specific high-stakes verticals (finance, healthcare, defense) where the threat model justifies the cost. The mainstream of distributed databases will not adopt BFT broadly. The middle ground (some BFT properties retrofitted into crash-failure systems, e.g., signed AppendEntries, audit logs) is more likely than wholesale BFT adoption.

A second consideration: the cloud providers themselves have an incentive to address the trust gap via "confidential computing" (Intel SGX, AMD SEV, AWS Nitro Enclaves) that lets customers process data without the cloud provider seeing it. This is a different solution to the same threat model and may dominate over BFT for the cloud-trust scenario.

**Q2.** An LLM is asked to design a "high-security distributed system." It produces a design that uses BFT consensus. Identify three things the LLM probably did not consider, and explain why "use BFT" is rarely the complete answer.

**Discussion:**

(a) **Where do the BFT replicas live?** BFT tolerates fff compromised nodes but the math only works if the fff compromised nodes do not include enough of the same physical infrastructure. A 3f+1 replica set hosted in one DC defeats the BFT model the moment that DC is compromised. The geographic/organizational distribution of replicas matters as much as the protocol.

(b) **Key management.** BFT relies on cryptographic signatures. The keys must be managed: rotated, revoked when compromised, kept out of the same trust boundary as the replicas. Most LLM-generated designs gloss over key management, but it is often the actual security weak point.

(c) **Side-channel resistance.** A nominally-honest replica that is observable (timing side channels, cache side channels) can leak information that breaks the protocol's privacy or integrity assumptions. Real high-security designs need side-channel-resistant implementations, which most languages and libraries do not provide by default.

Three more (any of which makes "use BFT" insufficient):

(d) **Client authentication.** BFT protects the replicas from each other but not the protocol from a malicious client. The client interface needs its own authentication and authorization layer.

(e) **Bootstrap trust.** When the system first starts, how do replicas know each other's identities? The initial trust anchor (CA, hardcoded keys, trusted setup) is often the weak point.

(f) **Operational compromise.** A BFT system whose operators (the team running the replicas) can collude defeats the BFT model. Real high-security deployments need separation of duties at the operations level, which is an organizational design problem, not a technical one.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 10: Beyond Classic Paxos — HotStuff, Narwhal-Bullshark, Flexible Quorums
blocks.src:
The deeper observation: "high security" is an organizational property, not a protocol property. BFT is one tool; it must be combined with key management, geographic distribution, side-channel resistance, organizational separation, and many other practices. An LLM that produces "use BFT" as the answer to "high security" is giving a partial answer; the complete answer requires expertise the LLM does not have.


### Chapter Summary

Byzantine Fault Tolerance handles arbitrary node misbehavior, including malicious behavior, equivocation, and corrupted state. The cost is 3f+13f + 13f+1 replicas (vs 2f+12f + 12f+1 for crash-only) and cryptographic signatures on protocol messages.

PBFT was the classical practical BFT protocol; its O(N2)O(N^2)O(N2) message complexity limited it to small replica sets. HotStuff (2019) achieved O(N)O(N)O(N) view change via Quorum Certificates and pipelining, making BFT practical for hundreds of replicas. Narwhal-Bullshark (2022) separated mempool from consensus via a DAG structure, raising throughput further. Tendermint is the simpler workhorse used by the Cosmos ecosystem.

Heidi Howard's Flexible Paxos generalized the quorum requirement: only intersection between prepare and accept quorums is needed, not majority of each. This lets operators tune for fast-common-case with slow-rare-case.

Non-blockchain BFT use cases include cloud control planes under attack, cross-organizational data sharing, and high-stakes configuration stores. For most systems, the cost of BFT outweighs the benefit and crash-failure consensus is appropriate.

Chapter 11 begins Part IV on distributed databases. The protocols of Chapters 7-10 are the foundation; databases like Spanner, CockroachDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, and FoundationDB are the production systems that build on the foundation. The chapter teaches the _diagnostic method_ : how to read any distributed database's CAP and PACELC position in 30 minutes by identifying its replication protocol, failure-recovery semantics, consistency model, and partition behavior.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
Olamide is sitting across from her CTO. The CTO has 30 minutes before the next meeting. The question on the table: should Crescent migrate its payment ledger from PostgreSQL to CockroachDB?

Olamide does not have time to read CockroachDB's documentation cover to cover. She does not need to. She has a diagnostic method, and the method works in 30 minutes for any distributed database that has ever been deployed in production.

This chapter teaches that method. The method is four questions, in order. By the end, you can read Spanner, CockroachDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, or FoundationDB and produce a one-page reading that says what each system is, what it costs, when it fails, and what it was designed for.


### 11.1 The Four Questions

For any distributed database, ask:

  1. **What is the replication protocol?** Single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless, quorum-based, consensus-based, custom.
  2. **What is the failure-recovery semantics?** Leader re-election (how long), gossip-based convergence, manual intervention.
  3. **What is the consistency model?** Linearizable, serializable, snapshot, causal, eventual, tunable per-operation.
  4. **What is the partition behavior?** Refuse-writes-minority, serve-stale, sloppy quorum, application-controlled.

These four questions, answered concretely, give you the system's PACELC profile, its operational characteristics, and its failure modes. They take 30 minutes to answer for any system because each has a definitive answer documented in the vendor's literature.


### 11.2 The Method, in Detail


#### Question 1: Replication Protocol

Read the system's documentation for "replication," "consensus," "consistency," or "high availability." Look for:

* **Single-leader** : PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB. The leader serializes writes; followers replicate asynchronously or via a configurable quorum.
* **Consensus-based per-shard** : CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB. Each shard (range, region, key range) has its own consensus group, typically Raft.
* **Consensus-based per-tablet with leases** : Spanner. Each tablet uses Paxos; the leader holds a lease for fast linearizable reads.
* **Leaderless** : Cassandra, DynamoDB, Riak. Any node accepts writes; conflicts resolved at read time or via background repair.
* **Custom** : Aurora (the storage layer is its own protocol; the database tier is single-leader); FoundationDB (a sequencer-based design).

The protocol determines the write latency, the failover behavior, and the conflict-resolution mechanism. It is the most important property of the system.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### Question 2: Failure-Recovery Semantics

How does the system handle node failure? Specifically:

* **Leader re-election timing** : Raft-based systems typically 1-5 seconds; etcd is fast (sub-second under good conditions); Spanner's Paxos with leases is similar. PostgreSQL's logical failover requires external tooling (Patroni, repmgr) and is 10-60 seconds.
* **Gossip-based convergence** : Cassandra detects node failure via gossip (10-30 seconds default). Failed nodes are excluded from quorum decisions during that window; the system makes do with the surviving nodes.
* **Split-brain prevention** : most consensus-based systems prevent split-brain automatically (the minority side cannot get quorum). Leaderless systems prevent split-brain via quorum (W + R > N). Single-leader systems (Postgres) can split-brain without external coordination.
* **Manual intervention required** : legacy systems and some replication setups require human action to promote a replica. The RTO is measured in hours.

The failure-recovery timing determines the availability SLA. A system with 5-second Raft re-elections has a different downtime profile than one with 60-second Patroni failover.


#### Question 3: Consistency Model

What does the system guarantee for individual operations? The model can be one of:

* **Linearizable** (the strongest single-operation property): every operation appears to take effect instantaneously at some point between invocation and response, consistent with real-time order. Spanner, CockroachDB (default for transactions), TiDB.
* **Serializable** (the strongest transactional property): transactions are equivalent to some serial order. CockroachDB (transaction-level), TiDB. Note: serializable is _not_ the same as linearizable; serializable orders transactions, linearizable orders operations in real-time.
* **Snapshot isolation** : transactions see a consistent snapshot but write-write conflicts are not prevented (write skew is possible). PostgreSQL (REPEATABLE READ in practice; SERIALIZABLE is a stricter variant). CockroachDB before its 2.0 default change.
* **Causal** : writes-follow-reads, read-your-writes preserved across sessions. Some Cassandra configurations, some MongoDB configurations.
* **Eventual** : replicas converge eventually; reads may see stale data. Cassandra (default), DynamoDB (default), Riak.
* **Tunable per-operation** : the application chooses per-request. Cassandra (consistency levels), DynamoDB (consistent reads on request), Spanner (stale reads available).

The consistency model determines what bugs the application can avoid for free vs what it must handle explicitly.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### Question 4: Partition Behavior

When a network partition occurs, what does each side of the partition do?

* **Refuse writes on minority side** (CP under partition): Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB. The minority side stops accepting writes; the majority side continues.
* **Serve all reads from any side, accept writes anywhere** (AP under partition): Cassandra with default consistency, DynamoDB with default consistency. Writes may conflict; conflict resolution (LWW, CRDT) decides outcome.
* **Sloppy quorum** (a Dynamo-specific behavior): when the primary replicas are unreachable, write to any reachable node (hinted handoff); read from any quorum. The intersection guarantee can break.
* **Application-controlled** : Cassandra with tunable consistency, DynamoDB with optional consistent reads. The application chooses per-request which behavior it wants.

The partition behavior is the worst-case behavior; PACELC's "P" half. Combined with the normal-operation cost (the "EL"/"EC" half of PACELC), this gives the full profile.


### 11.3 The Five-System Walkthrough — Workflow 6: Reading a Database in 30 Minutes

> **Workflow 6 (input → output)** : given any distributed database's documentation, produce a one-page PACELC + operational profile (replication protocol, failure-recovery semantics, consistency model, partition behavior) within 30 minutes. The mechanism is the four-question diagnostic of §11.1-§11.2; the output is the kind of table shown in §11.3 for Spanner / CockroachDB / DynamoDB / Cassandra / FoundationDB. Variations: apply the same method to message queues, caches, search engines, ML inference clusters — the four questions generalize. The skill being trained: read vendor documentation through the lens of structural properties, not marketing claims; produce a defensible judgment on whether the system fits a specific workload.

Olamide applies the method to five systems. The output is the one-page reading for each.


#### Spanner (Google)

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Paxos per tablet; TrueTime-based commit-wait for linearizable timestamps  
Failure-recovery | Paxos leader re-election (~seconds); TrueTime infrastructure (GPS + atomic clocks) makes leader-lease reads fast  
Consistency model | Linearizable for read-write transactions; stale-bounded reads available for read-only  
Partition behavior | CP — minority side stops accepting writes; TrueTime ensures consistent timestamps post-partition  
PACELC | PC / EC (consistent under partition; pays commit-wait latency in normal operation)  
Strengths | Global linearizability without restart cost; mature operational story; multi-region  
Weaknesses | GCP-only (no AWS/Azure availability); expensive; commit-wait latency baked into every write  
Right for | Workloads where global linearizability is required (ad serving, financial ledger); Google's own infrastructure

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### CockroachDB

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Raft per range; HLC-based MVCC for linearizable timestamps via NTP-skew bound (default 500 ms)  
Failure-recovery | Raft leader re-election (sub-second to seconds); per-range leadership transfer  
Consistency model | Serializable transactions; reads at HLC-aware bounded staleness on followers  
Partition behavior | CP — minority side stops accepting writes  
PACELC | PC / EC (consistent under partition; pays HLC-restart cost on uncertainty-window reads)  
Strengths | Postgres-compatible SQL; deployable on any cloud; per-range Raft scales horizontally  
Weaknesses | Higher per-write latency than single-region Postgres; complex operational tuning  
Right for | Multi-region Postgres replacement; financial workloads requiring serializability  
  

#### DynamoDB (AWS)

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Leaderless within region; cross-region async replication for global tables  
Failure-recovery | Transparent (the storage layer is opaque to the user); auto-scaling and auto-repair  
Consistency model | Eventually consistent by default; strongly consistent reads available on request  
Partition behavior | AP under partition for default reads; conditional writes provide per-item linearizability  
PACELC | PA / EL by default (low latency, eventual); PC / EC for conditional-write operations  
Strengths | Hands-off operations; very predictable latency; integrates with AWS ecosystem  
Weaknesses | AWS-only; pricing model penalizes hot keys; data modeling constraints  
Right for | Single-tenant key-value workloads with predictable access patterns; AWS-native systems  
  

#### Cassandra

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Leaderless; tunable consistency per request (ONE, QUORUM, ALL)  
Failure-recovery | Gossip-based; nodes excluded after timeout; manual coordinator-failure handling  
Consistency model | Tunable per-operation; eventual by default, linearizable via LWT (Paxos-backed)  
Partition behavior | Tunable per-operation; AP at low consistency, CP at quorum  
PACELC | Tunable; PA / EL at low consistency, PC / EC at quorum  
Strengths | Linear scale-out to thousands of nodes; tunable trade-off  
Weaknesses | Operational complexity (tombstone management, compaction tuning); LWT is slow  
Right for | Write-heavy workloads with relaxed consistency; massive scale where per-node simplicity is the goal  
  

#### FoundationDB

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Custom (sequencer + transaction-log + storage); strongly consistent  
Failure-recovery | Fast (sub-second sequencer change); designed for chaos engineering from day one  
Consistency model | Serializable transactions; ACID with strong serializability guarantees  
Partition behavior | CP — refuses writes if quorum lost  
PACELC | PC / EC; designed for OLTP latency  
Strengths | Battle-tested correctness (Snowflake builds on it; Apple uses it heavily); chaos-engineered  
Weaknesses | Low-level API (the SQL layer is a separate project); smaller ecosystem than Postgres-compatibles  
Right for | Building distributed databases on top of (Snowflake's metadata layer); ACID workloads with high reliability requirements

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
### 11.4 Olamide's Decision

Olamide synthesizes for her CTO:

> "For the Crescent payment workload, the choice is between Spanner and CockroachDB. Both are PC/EC; both give us multi-region linearizability. Spanner is more mature but locks us to GCP. CockroachDB is Postgres-compatible (which our team knows) and runs on any cloud. The migration cost from Postgres-compatible code is lower. CockroachDB it is.
> 
> "DynamoDB is out: the consistency model requires per-operation discipline that our team is not ready to maintain for financial workloads. Cassandra is out: the tunable consistency is powerful but the operational burden is wrong for a payment system. FoundationDB is interesting but the lack of SQL layer means significant rework."

The CTO has the decision in 30 minutes. The reasoning is defensible. The migration plan can now be drafted, with full understanding of what the team is moving to and away from.

This is the method. Apply it before adopting any new database; apply it before reading any blog post that claims a system "is better than X."


### 11.5 Anya's Stratus DB Reading

Anya applies the same method to her own system in development. The reading:

Question | Answer (Stratus DB)  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Raft per range (using raft-rs); HLC-based MVCC  
Failure-recovery | Per-range Raft re-election (~1 second); regional failover via consensus  
Consistency model | Serializable transactions; follower reads with bounded staleness  
Partition behavior | CP — minority side refuses writes  
PACELC | PC / EC  
Strengths | Built for financial workloads from day one; deep observability  
Weaknesses | New; ecosystem is small; SQL layer in development  
Right for | CockroachDB-style workloads, internal use at Stratus's partner companies  
  
The reading helps Anya communicate the system's profile to potential customers. Customers do not need to read CockroachDB-vs-Stratus comparisons; they need the method to evaluate either against their workload.


### 11.6 Common Pitfalls in Reading Documentation

(a) **Marketing-grade "consistency" claims**. Many vendors call themselves "consistent" without specifying which model. "Strongly consistent" can mean linearizable, serializable, snapshot, or something custom. Push for the precise model.

(b) **Conflating CAP and PACELC**. A vendor that says "CP" tells you the partition behavior but not the normal-operation cost. Always ask the PACELC question (what does this cost in milliseconds per operation when there is no partition?).

(c) **Per-operation vs system-level claims**. A system may be linearizable for some operations and eventual for others. The system-level label averages across this; the per-operation breakdown is what matters.

(d) **Marketing-grade availability claims**. "99.99% availability" is a SLA claim; the actual availability under partition is a different number. The CAP/PACELC analysis is the predictor.

(e) **Benchmarks at idealized conditions**. Vendor benchmarks are on optimal hardware, idealized network, single-region. Real production performance is 2-10x worse. The CAP/PACELC profile tells you what to expect when the network is bad.


### 11.7 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** State the four questions of the diagnostic method.

Hint

Replication protocol, failure-recovery, consistency model, partition behavior.

**Answer:**

  1. What is the replication protocol? (single-leader, multi-leader, leaderless, consensus-based, custom)
  2. What is the failure-recovery semantics? (re-election timing, gossip, manual)
  3. What is the consistency model? (linearizable, serializable, snapshot, causal, eventual, tunable)
  4. What is the partition behavior? (refuse minority, serve all, sloppy quorum, application-controlled)

Answering these four for any system produces the PACELC profile, the operational characteristics, and the failure modes.

**Q2.** What is the difference between "linearizable" and "serializable"?

Hint

Linearizable: real-time order respected; per-operation. Serializable: some serial order; per-transaction.

**Answer:** Linearizable is a per-operation property: every operation appears to take effect at some instant between its invocation and its response, consistent with real-time. If operation A completes (returns to caller) before operation B starts (caller invokes B), then A is ordered before B.

Serializable is a per-transaction property: any execution of concurrent transactions is equivalent to some serial order. The order need not be consistent with real-time; if transaction A returns before B starts, the serial-equivalent order may still place B before A.

For example, in a serializable system: transaction A writes x=1x = 1x=1 and commits at time 10. Transaction B reads xxx at time 20. The serializable property allows B to read the _old_ xxx (as if B were ordered before A in the serial equivalent), as long as the overall execution is equivalent to some serial order.

Linearizable would forbid this: B started after A completed, so B must see A's write.

The cost: linearizable systems pay more (consensus per read, or commit-wait, or HLC restart) than serializable. Many workloads need serializability (correct under concurrency) but not linearizability (correct under real-time). Knowing the difference avoids over-paying.

**Q3.** Use the diagnostic method to produce a one-paragraph reading for a system you have not used. Pick any of: MongoDB, ScyllaDB, Aurora DSQL, TigerBeetle, Neon.

Hint

Look up the vendor docs; map the answers into the four-question grid; synthesize.

**Answer:** Example for Aurora DSQL (AWS, GA 2024):

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
Aurora DSQL is a serverless, distributed SQL database from AWS, designed as a Postgres-compatible Spanner-style system on AWS infrastructure. The replication protocol is built on Firecracker microVMs per tenant with a decoupled storage layer (writes go to a 6-replica storage quorum, ack on 4 of 6). Failure-recovery is transparent (Firecracker can re-spin in seconds, and the storage layer handles replica failure independently). The consistency model is strongly consistent serializable; reads can be at the leader (immediate) or at follower with bounded staleness. Partition behavior is CP at the storage layer (writes block if the storage quorum is lost). PACELC: PC under partition, EC under no-partition (the storage layer's quorum write costs ~5-10 ms beyond the local Postgres logic). Strengths: serverless billing; Postgres-compatible; multi-region available. Weaknesses: AWS-only; new (still being battle-tested); the Firecracker-per-tenant model is unusual and may have surprising operational characteristics. Right for: Postgres workloads that want to be multi-region and serverless without managing a CockroachDB cluster.

The method generalizes: read the vendor's docs, find the four answers, write the synthesis. 30 minutes per system.

**Q4.** Why is the diagnostic method better than reading vendor blog posts comparing two systems?

Hint

Comparisons are framed by the vendor's worldview; the method gives you the same framework for any system.

**Answer:** Vendor blog posts comparing systems are framed by the vendor's worldview. A CockroachDB blog post comparing CockroachDB to Postgres will emphasize CockroachDB's strengths and Postgres's weaknesses. A Postgres advocate's blog post will reverse the emphasis. Neither produces a balanced reading.

The diagnostic method:

(a) Produces the same framework for any system, so direct comparison is possible. (b) Forces concrete answers (you cannot dodge by saying "fast"; you must say "1 ms per single-region write at p50, 80 ms multi-region commit"). (c) Surfaces the trade-offs that the vendor would prefer not to emphasize. (d) Lets you compare systems on the dimensions your application cares about, not on the dimensions the vendor likes to compare.

For Crescent's decision: a Spanner-vs-CockroachDB blog post would not have addressed the GCP-lock-in concern (a vendor of one would not emphasize the lock-in disadvantage of the other; a vendor of the other would emphasize it disproportionately). The method surfaces this naturally because "what cloud is required" is part of the strengths/weaknesses synthesis.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Apply the diagnostic method to TigerBeetle. Read its documentation enough to answer the four questions, and produce a one-page reading.

Hint

TigerBeetle is a financial-grade ledger database designed for deterministic simulation testing and the TigerStyle programming discipline. Look for its replication protocol, failure model, consistency, and partition behavior.

**Answer:** TigerBeetle reading:

Question | Answer  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Custom Viewstamped Replication variant; 5-replica deployment is canonical; cluster-wide write sequencing  
Failure-recovery | Sub-second view-change; designed for deterministic simulation testing (every reachable state explicitly enumerated and exercised)  
Consistency model | Strict serializability for double-entry accounting transactions; linearizable per-transfer  
Partition behavior | CP — refuses writes on minority side; quorum is majority of replicas  
PACELC | PC / EC; optimized for financial OLTP throughput (claims 1M+ transfers per second in benchmark)  
Strengths | Financial-grade correctness model (deterministic simulation testing + TigerStyle programming); deterministic execution; debugging-friendly  
Weaknesses | Specialized for double-entry accounting (not general-purpose); small ecosystem  
Right for | Banking ledgers, payment systems, financial OLTP where the schema fits TigerBeetle's accounting model  
  
TigerBeetle is interesting as a study in domain-specific design: by restricting the data model (double-entry only), the system can be much faster and much more verifiable than a general-purpose database. Crescent's payment ledger could use TigerBeetle for the actual transfer recording (the schema fits) while using CockroachDB for the user-facing metadata. This is a real architectural pattern in 2026 finance systems.

**Q2.** A team is evaluating MongoDB for a new microservice. They ask: "Is MongoDB consistent?" Use the diagnostic method to give a precise, defensible answer.

Hint

MongoDB's consistency depends on configuration: writeConcern, readConcern, replica set vs sharded. The default is not the same as the strongest available.

**Answer:** MongoDB's consistency depends heavily on configuration. The precise answer requires specifying which operations and which configuration.

For a replica set (3-node typical):

* _Default write_ : `writeConcern: 1` (single-node ack). Eventually consistent for replication; can be lost if the primary crashes before replication.
* _Majority write_ : `writeConcern: majority`. The write is durable to a majority before ack; survives primary failure.
* _Default read_ : `readConcern: local` from primary. Linearizable for primary reads, eventually consistent from secondaries (which are the default for reads from MongoDB clients with `readPreference: secondary`).
* _Majority read_ : `readConcern: majority` returns data acknowledged by a majority.
* _Linearizable read_ : `readConcern: linearizable` provides linearizability for reads. Available since MongoDB 3.4.

For a sharded cluster: each shard is a replica set; the above applies per shard. Cross-shard transactions are available (MongoDB 4.0+) and provide snapshot isolation across shards.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
Defensible precise answer: "MongoDB can be made linearizable per-operation with `writeConcern: majority, readConcern: linearizable` in a replica set. The default configuration is eventually consistent (writeConcern 1, read from secondary). Cross-shard transactions provide snapshot isolation. The team must consciously choose the consistency level appropriate to each operation; the system's default is not the strongest level available."

This is the correct shape of answer: precise about which configuration, which operation, what guarantee. Saying "MongoDB is consistent" is meaningless; saying "MongoDB can be linearizable with this configuration" is actionable.

**Q3.** A startup is choosing between Cassandra and ScyllaDB for an analytics workload. Apply the diagnostic method to both, then synthesize the recommendation.

Hint

ScyllaDB is Cassandra-compatible but written in C++ with shard-per-core. Same protocol family, different implementation; compare on performance, operational characteristics.

**Answer:** Both systems have the same diagnostic profile (they share the protocol):

Question | Answer (both)  
---|---  
Replication protocol | Leaderless; tunable consistency per request  
Failure-recovery | Gossip-based; node exclusion after timeout  
Consistency model | Tunable: eventual by default, linearizable via LWT  
Partition behavior | Tunable; AP at low consistency, CP at quorum  
PACELC | Tunable; PA/EL or PC/EC depending on per-operation config  
  
The differences are in the implementation:

Aspect | Cassandra | ScyllaDB  
---|---|---  
Implementation | Java (JVM) | C++ (shard-per-core)  
Memory profile | Heap-bound (GC pauses) | Heap-free (no GC pauses)  
Per-node throughput | ~50,000 ops/sec | ~500,000 ops/sec  
Operational complexity | High (compaction tuning, GC tuning) | Moderate (architecture handles much of it)  
Ecosystem | Larger (older project) | Growing; Cassandra-compatible APIs  
Cost | Open source; many cloud-managed offerings | Open source + ScyllaDB Cloud  
  
Synthesis for an analytics workload (typically high-throughput, eventual-consistency tolerant):

ScyllaDB is the right answer if (a) per-node throughput matters (you want fewer, more powerful nodes), (b) GC pauses are a problem (latency-sensitive analytics), (c) the operational team is comfortable with C++-stack debugging. Cassandra is the right answer if (a) the team already knows it deeply, (b) the broader ecosystem matters (existing Cassandra-aware tooling), (c) the per-node throughput is not the bottleneck.

For a new startup with no prior commitment, ScyllaDB is likely the better default in 2026 for new analytics workloads. The 10x per-node throughput advantage means fewer nodes, simpler topology, lower cost. The diagnostic method (both systems have the same logical profile) shows you do not lose anything by switching the implementation.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "The diagnostic method is incomplete because it doesn't include cost, ecosystem, and operational experience. These often dominate the technical evaluation."

**Discussion:** The defense (the claim is right): cost, ecosystem, and operational experience are usually the dominant factors in real-world database adoption. The diagnostic method gives you the technical reading but not the business reading. A team that picks the technically-best system without considering cost or operational maturity often regrets the choice.

The refutation (the method is sufficient): the diagnostic method is intentionally scoped to technical evaluation. Adding cost, ecosystem, and operational experience as "questions" would make the method longer and less applicable across systems. The right model is: use the diagnostic method to produce the technical reading, then layer the business considerations on top.

The synthesis: the method as presented is the _technical_ part of the evaluation. The full evaluation also includes (i) cost (cloud bill, license, infrastructure), (ii) ecosystem (existing tooling, hiring pool, third-party support), (iii) operational experience (team's prior knowledge, incident history with the technology), (iv) strategic concerns (vendor lock-in, exit options). These factors are organization-specific and should be added by the evaluating team.

The Crescent decision example showed both layers: the technical method narrowed the choice to Spanner vs CockroachDB; the business layer (no GCP lock-in, Postgres-compatibility for the team's existing skills) made the final choice. Both layers are necessary; neither is sufficient.

**Q2.** An LLM is asked "which database is best?" without further context. It produces an answer. Why is the answer almost certainly wrong, and what should the LLM have asked before answering?

**Discussion:** "Best" has no meaning without a workload. The LLM, asked the question, has no information about:

* The workload's consistency requirement (linearizable, eventual, somewhere in between).
* The latency budget per operation.
* The deployment footprint (single region, multi region, cross-cloud).
* The cost budget.
* The team's existing expertise.
* The integration constraints (which other systems must this work with).
* The regulatory constraints (GDPR, data residency, audit).
* The scale (TB or PB; rows per second).

Without any of these, the LLM is producing an opinion based on the average of its training data, which over-represents popular systems (PostgreSQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB) and under-represents specialized systems that would be the right answer in specific contexts.

The LLM should have asked: "What does the workload need? What are your constraints? What are you trying to optimize for?" These are the same questions any human database consultant would ask.

The deeper observation: "best database" is the kind of question that has no answer without context, and an LLM that produces a confident answer is signaling that it does not understand the question. A more honest LLM would refuse to answer until given the context, or would produce an "if-then" answer mapping workload characteristics to database choices.

The diagnostic method is the bridge: once the LLM (or the human) knows the workload, the method narrows the field to a few candidates. Then domain expertise (or further questions) picks among them.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 11: Reading a Distributed Database — Diagnose Any System's CAP Position in 30 Minutes
blocks.src:
### Chapter Summary

The diagnostic method (four questions: replication protocol, failure-recovery, consistency, partition behavior) lets you read any distributed database's CAP and PACELC position in 30 minutes. The method generalizes; it works for systems you have never used because the four questions have definitive answers in any vendor's documentation.

Olamide's Crescent decision (CockroachDB over Spanner, DynamoDB, Cassandra, FoundationDB) is defensible because the method produces the same framework for all five systems and surfaces the trade-offs the vendors would prefer not to emphasize.

The method is technical; the full evaluation also includes cost, ecosystem, and operational experience. These business factors are layered on top of the technical reading; neither layer is sufficient alone.

Common pitfalls in reading documentation: marketing-grade "consistency" claims that conflate linearizable with serializable; conflating CAP and PACELC; per-operation vs system-level claims; idealized benchmarks. The method protects against these by demanding precise answers.

Chapter 12 takes the next layer: how distributed databases actually shard data across nodes. Hash partitioning, range partitioning, consistent hashing, the LSM-tree foundations of Bigtable / Cassandra / RocksDB, and Anya's worked example of a re-sharding migration without downtime on the Stratus DB cluster.

---

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
Anya is staring at a Slack message from her team's on-call: "Stratus cluster 7 is at 87% disk and growing 2% per day. Need to add capacity by end of next week."

The cluster has 12 nodes with 4 TB each (48 TB raw capacity), holding 42 TB of customer data at 87% utilization. The data is sharded by customer ID using consistent hashing. Adding nodes requires resharding: data movement from existing nodes to the new ones, with zero downtime, while the cluster continues to serve 50,000 transactions per second.

This is Workflow 7 from the syllabus: a re-sharding migration without downtime. Anya has done it three times before. The protocol is in her head; the operational discipline is in her runbook. This chapter walks through it, with the foundations (hash vs range partitioning, consistent hashing, LSM-trees) that make the protocol possible.


### 12.1 Hash vs Range Partitioning

Two fundamentally different ways to map keys to nodes.


#### Hash partitioning

Each key is hashed; the hash determines the partition (and therefore the node). The hash function is fixed; the mapping from key to partition is deterministic.

Pros:

* **Even load distribution** : a good hash function spreads keys uniformly across partitions, regardless of key skew.
* **Trivial routing** : any node can compute "which partition owns this key" without looking anything up.
* **No hot spots from sequential keys** : even if keys are sequential (incrementing user IDs), the hash scatters them.

Cons:

* **No range queries** : "give me all keys between A and Z" requires consulting every partition.
* **No range scan locality** : keys that are logically related (same user's data) may be on different partitions.

Used by: Dynamo, Cassandra (default partitioner: Murmur3Partitioner), Redis Cluster.


#### Range partitioning

Keys are sorted; each partition owns a contiguous range. The partition boundaries are stored in metadata (a coordinator, a routing table).

Pros:

* **Efficient range queries** : a range query touches only the partitions overlapping the range.
* **Locality** : logically-related keys (sorted by user ID) end up on the same partition.

Cons:

* **Hot spots from sequential keys** : incrementing IDs all land in the latest partition; that partition gets all writes until it splits.
* **Routing requires metadata lookup** : the client must know which range each partition holds; this metadata must be replicated and kept current.

Used by: HBase (HBase's reason for being is range scans over wide rows), CockroachDB (default), Spanner (per-tablet), TiKV.


#### The 2026 hybrid

Modern systems often offer both. CockroachDB's default is range partitioning, but a table can be explicitly hash-partitioned (with a `crdb_internal` shard key). Cassandra is hash-partitioned but offers "partition keys" plus "clustering columns" so that the data within a partition is sorted (giving local range queries within the hash partition).

The choice depends on the workload: pure-OLTP point lookups favor hash; analytical scans favor range; mixed workloads need both via per-table configuration.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
### 12.2 Consistent Hashing

The naive hash partitioning approach (key → hash mod N) has a fatal flaw: changing N (adding or removing nodes) re-hashes every key, requiring all data to move. For a 12-node cluster adding 1 node, 12/13 of data must move. This is operationally infeasible.

Consistent hashing, introduced by Karger and colleagues in their 1997 paper on web cache distribution, solves this. The idea:

* Map both nodes and keys onto a circular hash space (e.g., a 64-bit integer space, treated as a ring).
* Each key is owned by the _first node clockwise_ from the key's position on the ring.
* Adding a node: the new node takes responsibility for keys between itself and its clockwise neighbor. Only keys in that range move (not the whole dataset).
* Removing a node: the next clockwise node takes responsibility for the removed node's range. Same locality.

For NNN nodes uniformly placed, adding one node moves 1/(N+1)1/(N+1)1/(N+1) of the data. For N=12N = 12N=12, one new node moves about 1/13, or 7.7%. Tractable.


#### Virtual nodes (vnodes)

Naive consistent hashing has a load-imbalance problem: if a node happens to land in a sparse region of the ring, it owns a large range and gets disproportionate load. The fix: each physical node owns many "virtual nodes" (vnodes) scattered across the ring. Cassandra defaults to 256 vnodes per physical node; this gives much more uniform load distribution.

Vnodes also help with rebalancing: when a new node joins, it takes vnodes from many existing nodes, spreading the rebalance cost across the cluster instead of concentrating it on one neighbor.


### 12.3 Range Partitioning in Practice

CockroachDB's range partitioning is the modern reference design.

* The keyspace is divided into _ranges_ , each typically 64-512 MB of data.
* Each range has its own Raft group (3 replicas in a 3-replica deployment).
* A coordinator (the system metadata) tracks which range covers which key span.
* When a range grows past a threshold, it _splits_ (the range is divided into two; each half becomes a new range with its own Raft group).
* When a range shrinks too small, it _merges_ with a neighbor.
* When load is uneven, the system _rebalances_ by moving replicas between physical nodes.

The metadata is itself a range (a special range), so it is consistent and replicated. Clients cache the routing table and refresh on misses. The system can handle thousands of range splits per minute under sustained growth.

The split mechanism is the key: a hot range (one receiving disproportionate traffic) automatically splits, distributing the load. Cassandra cannot do this; its hash partitioning means a hot key stays on one partition until the application changes the key.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
### 12.4 LSM-Trees: The Storage Substrate

Most modern distributed databases store data in _LSM-trees_ (Log-Structured Merge-trees). LSM-trees were introduced by O'Neil and colleagues in 1996 and popularized by Bigtable — described by Chang and colleagues in their 2006 OSDI paper — then adopted by Cassandra, RocksDB, ScyllaDB, LevelDB, and many others.

The LSM structure:

(a) **Memtable** : an in-memory sorted structure (skip list, red-black tree). New writes go here first.

(b) **Write-ahead log (WAL)** : every write is also appended to a durable log on disk before going to the memtable. Crash recovery replays the WAL.

(c) **SSTable (Sorted String Table)** : when the memtable fills up, it is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file. New writes start filling a new memtable.

(d) **Compaction** : periodically, multiple SSTables are merged into a smaller number of larger SSTables. This reclaims space (deleted keys are dropped), reduces the number of files to consult on reads, and keeps the on-disk structure organized.


#### Why LSM beats B-tree for write-heavy workloads

A B-tree update requires reading the relevant page (4-16 KB), modifying it, and writing it back. Random writes have high I/O cost on traditional spinning disks; SSDs handle them better but still pay a write-amplification cost.

An LSM update is just an append to the memtable (in-memory; fast) and an append to the WAL (sequential write; fast). The compaction work happens asynchronously, batched. For write-heavy workloads, LSM trades immediate write efficiency for periodic compaction overhead.

The trade-off:

* **Write throughput** : LSM wins (often 10-100x for sustained writes).
* **Read latency** : B-tree wins for point lookups (one page read; LSM may need to check multiple SSTables and the memtable, with Bloom filters helping).
* **Range scan** : comparable; LSM's sorted-merge is similar to B-tree's leaf-traversal.
* **Space amplification** : LSM can have 1.5-3x space overhead (multiple SSTables before compaction); B-tree is closer to 1x.

In 2026, LSM dominates the distributed-database storage substrate because most workloads are write-heavy or write-throughput-limited. Bigtable, Cassandra, RocksDB (used as engine by CockroachDB, TiKV, YugabyteDB, MongoDB WiredTiger optionally), ScyllaDB, LevelDB, and many others use LSM.


#### Compaction strategies

Two main compaction strategies:

* **Size-tiered compaction** : when a level has enough similarly-sized SSTables, merge them into a larger one. Used by Cassandra's default.
* **Leveled compaction** : maintain SSTables in size-stratified levels; each level is N times larger than the previous. Used by LevelDB, RocksDB.

Size-tiered is faster (less write amplification) but has higher space amplification (more SSTables coexist). Leveled is more space-efficient (more aggressive merging) but pays more write amplification. The choice depends on workload: write-heavy with cheap disk = size-tiered; read-heavy with expensive disk = leveled.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
#### Common Misconception

A common confusion: "LSM is for write-heavy workloads; B-tree is for read-heavy." Partially true but oversimplified. LSM's read performance is competitive with B-tree for many workloads (point lookups with Bloom filters; range scans benefit from sorted SSTables). The real distinction is the write path: LSM converts random writes into sequential writes (via the WAL and memtable batching), which is a structural advantage that B-trees cannot match. For modern workloads on SSDs, the LSM advantage is the _predictable_ write throughput; the read performance is usually adequate.


### 12.5 Workflow 7: Anya's Resharding Migration

Now Anya's specific problem: 12-node cluster at 87% disk, needs to add 3 nodes by next week, while serving 50,000 TPS with no downtime.

Anya's protocol:


#### Step 1: Provision and join the new nodes

The 3 new nodes are provisioned with the same software, same configuration. They join the cluster as members (the cluster's coordinator service is told about them).

The new nodes do not yet own any data; they are spare capacity.


#### Step 2: Rebalance the metadata

The cluster's range table is updated: ranges that were on overloaded nodes are reassigned (in metadata) to the new nodes. The reassignment is lazy: the data has not yet moved.

For Stratus's 12-node cluster adding 3, the rebalance algorithm targets each node holding ~1/15 of the ranges. Currently, each of the 12 holds 1/12. The new target moves about 20% of the existing data to the new nodes (3/15 of total = 20%, divided evenly from the old 12).


#### Step 3: Stream the data

For each range that is being reassigned, the source node sends a _snapshot_ to the destination node. The source continues serving reads and writes during the snapshot; new writes are buffered to be sent after the snapshot completes.

For LSM-backed storage, the snapshot is an efficient SSTable copy: the source's SSTable files for the range are streamed to the destination. New writes (since the snapshot point) are applied via the Raft log replay.

The destination, once it has caught up, signals the source. The Raft group's leadership for the range is transferred to the destination, and the source's replica is removed.


#### Step 4: Validate

After the rebalance completes, the cluster monitors for:

* Even load distribution (queries-per-second per node).
* Even disk usage.
* Raft group health (no stuck replicas, no underreplication).

If any range got "stuck" (e.g., a Raft group fell behind during the move), the operator intervenes. In Anya's three previous reshardings, this happened twice; each took 10 minutes to resolve.


#### Step 5: Decommission old hardware (if applicable)

For this rebalance, no decommissioning. (Some reshardings are about replacing old hardware; the procedure is similar but the source node is being removed entirely.)


#### Time budget

For 42 TB total, moving 20% (8.4 TB) at 100 MB/s per stream (the cluster has 4 streams in parallel; 400 MB/s aggregate):

8.4 TB/400 MB/s≈21,000 seconds≈5.8 hours8.4 \text{ TB} / 400 \text{ MB/s} \approx 21,000 \text{ seconds} \approx 5.8 \text{ hours}8.4 TB/400 MB/s≈21,000 seconds≈5.8 hours

In practice, the move is throttled to avoid impacting customer traffic; the actual wall-clock time is 12-18 hours. Anya schedules the move overnight; by morning, the cluster is rebalanced and the disk usage is around 70% per node (42 TB spread over 15 × 4 TB = 60 TB → 70%).

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
#### What went right

(a) The protocol is online: customers experience no downtime.

(b) The cluster's transactional consistency is preserved throughout (Raft handles the per-range leadership transfer; the cluster's strong consistency does not lapse).

(c) The protocol is reversible: if a problem is detected mid-move, the move can be paused and the in-flight state rolled back.

(d) The protocol is parallelizable: multiple ranges move concurrently, bounded by network and disk throughput.


#### What can go wrong

(a) **Range size estimation error** : if the system's metadata about range size is stale, the rebalance plan can move too much or too little data. The fix is periodic re-estimation, which the cluster does hourly.

(b) **Replication lag during stream** : if the network is saturated, the destination's catch-up via Raft log replay takes longer than expected. The fix is to throttle other traffic during the move.

(c) **Node failure during move** : a failed source node (or destination) requires re-planning the move. The cluster's Raft groups continue serving (the per-range majority is unaffected), so the user-visible impact is brief degradation.

The discipline is operational: the runbook is the codification of years of these moves going slightly wrong. Anya's runbook has 47 checklist items; she ticks them off methodically.


### 12.6 B+ Trees as the Alternative

LSM-trees dominate the modern distributed-database storage substrate, but B+ trees (the variant of B-trees that stores data only in leaves) are not obsolete. Where B+ trees still win:

* **Postgres** : B+ tree index by default. Mature, well-understood.
* **MySQL InnoDB** : B+ tree.
* **SQL Server, Oracle** : B+ tree primary storage.

B+ tree strengths:

* Predictable read latency (one root-to-leaf path; bounded depth).
* Low space amplification.
* Mature operational tooling (decades of optimization).

B+ tree weaknesses:

* Random write cost (each update potentially modifies a different page).
* Page-level locking (or MVCC overhead).

The modern verdict: for OLTP workloads dominated by reads with relatively low write rates, B+ trees in a single-node database remain excellent. For high-write-throughput workloads, especially distributed, LSM is the right substrate.


### 12.7 Exercises

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Distinguish hash partitioning from range partitioning. Give one workload where each is the right choice.

Hint

Hash spreads load evenly but can't do range queries; range supports scans but has hot-spot risk on sequential keys.

**Answer:** Hash partitioning hashes each key; the hash determines the partition. Even load distribution, trivial routing, no range queries.

Range partitioning sorts keys; each partition owns a contiguous range. Efficient range queries, locality for related keys, hot-spot risk for sequential writes.

Hash is right for: a key-value store of user sessions, where each session is accessed by ID and there are no range queries. Examples: Redis Cluster, DynamoDB.

Range is right for: a time-series database that often queries "all events between time T1 and T2." Range partitioning by timestamp makes the query a single-partition scan. Examples: HBase, ClickHouse, TimescaleDB.

Many modern systems offer both per-table: CockroachDB defaults to range but supports hash-partitioned tables; Cassandra is hash-partitioned but allows sorted clustering within a partition for local range queries.

**Q2.** Why is consistent hashing better than "hash mod N" for distributed key-value storage?

Hint

Adding or removing a node with hash-mod-N moves most data; consistent hashing moves only ~1/N.

**Answer:** With hash-mod-N partitioning, every key's partition is determined by `hash(key) mod N`. If NNN changes (adding or removing a node), the mapping changes for almost every key. For N=12→13N = 12 \to 13N=12→13, 12/13 of keys map to a different partition; almost all data must move.

With consistent hashing, keys and nodes are placed on a ring; each key is owned by the next clockwise node. Adding a node inserts it into the ring; only the keys between the new node and its clockwise neighbor must move. For N=12→13N = 12 \to 13N=12→13, about 1/13 of data moves (the range that the new node now owns).

The operational implication: cluster resizing is feasible with consistent hashing (move 8% of data) but infeasible with hash-mod-N (move 92% of data). Every modern distributed key-value system uses some form of consistent hashing or its descendants.

Virtual nodes (vnodes) further refine: each physical node owns many vnodes scattered across the ring. This gives more uniform load distribution and spreads rebalance cost across many neighbors.

**Q3.** Describe the LSM-tree write path. Why is it faster than a B+ tree write?

Hint

LSM: write to WAL (sequential), write to memtable (in-memory). B+ tree: read page, modify, write back (random I/O).

**Answer:** LSM write path:

  1. The write is appended to the WAL (write-ahead log) on disk. This is a sequential write.
  2. The write is inserted into the memtable (in-memory sorted structure). This is fast.
  3. When the memtable fills, it is flushed to disk as an immutable SSTable.
  4. Periodically, multiple SSTables are merged via compaction.

The user-visible write completes after steps 1 and 2; subsequent compaction is asynchronous.

B+ tree write path:

  1. The write must update the relevant leaf page (4-16 KB on disk).
  2. The leaf page is read (random I/O if not cached).
  3. The page is modified in memory.
  4. The page is written back (another I/O).
  5. If the page is full, it splits, requiring updates to the parent (and potentially the root).

Why LSM is faster for writes:

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
(a) LSM writes are _sequential_ (WAL append; flushing whole memtable as a new SSTable). Sequential writes are 10-100x faster than random writes on traditional storage, and faster (but less dramatically) on SSDs.

(b) LSM batches the disk I/O: many writes accumulate in the memtable before flushing. B+ tree must touch the disk per-page-update.

(c) LSM amortizes compaction cost: the merging happens asynchronously, not on the user's write path.

For sustained high write throughput, LSM is structurally superior to B+ tree. For point reads, B+ tree has lower latency (one I/O); LSM needs to check multiple SSTables (Bloom filters help).

**Q4.** Why does Cassandra default to 256 vnodes per physical node? What problem does this solve?

Hint

Load distribution. Without vnodes, a single physical node can land in a sparse part of the ring and get disproportionate load.

**Answer:** With naive consistent hashing (one position per physical node), the load on each node is the size of its "arc" on the ring (from itself to the next clockwise node). Random placement means some nodes' arcs are much larger than others; a node with a 2x arc gets 2x the load.

For 12 randomly-placed nodes, the largest arc is typically 2-3x the average. This means the most-loaded node has 2-3x the queries-per-second of the average node, with corresponding disk and CPU pressure.

With 256 vnodes per physical node, each physical node has 256 random positions on the ring. The aggregate "arc" owned by one physical node is the sum of 256 random arcs, which by the law of large numbers is close to the expected value (1/N of the ring). Load distribution is much more uniform.

A second benefit: when a new physical node joins, it takes vnodes from many existing physical nodes (because the new node's 256 vnodes are scattered). The data movement is spread across the cluster, not concentrated on one or two neighbors. This makes rebalancing faster and gentler.

256 is a parameter; the right value depends on cluster size. Larger clusters can use fewer vnodes per node (1024 vnodes for a 100-node cluster gives 10 vnodes per node, which is enough). Smaller clusters need more vnodes per node for good distribution. 256 is Cassandra's default because it balances uniformity with token-management overhead for typical cluster sizes.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Anya's cluster is 12 × 4 TB nodes at 87% disk. She needs to add 3 nodes (same 4 TB capacity each). Walk through the time budget for the resharding, assuming the cluster has 4 parallel streams at 100 MB/s each.

Hint

~8.4 TB of data must move. Each of the 12 old nodes holds 87% × 4 TB ≈ 3.5 TB; after adding 3 nodes, the target drops to 42 TB / 15 = 2.8 TB per node, so each old node sheds 0.7 TB. Aggregate throughput is 400 MB/s. Throttle for production traffic.

**Answer:** Current state: 12 nodes × 4 TB capacity × 87% ≈ 12 × 3.5 TB = 42 TB total data. After adding 3 nodes (same 4 TB each): 15 × 4 TB = 60 TB total capacity. Target per-node usage: 42 TB / 15 = 2.8 TB. Each old node sheds: 3.5 − 2.8 = 0.7 TB. New nodes each receive: 8.4 TB / 3 = 2.8 TB — fits in 4 TB capacity.

Total data to move: 12 × 0.7 TB = 8.4 TB.

Time at 400 MB/s aggregate (4 streams × 100 MB/s):

8.4 TB=8400 GB=8,400,000 MB8.4 \text{ TB} = 8400 \text{ GB} = 8,400,000 \text{ MB}8.4 TB=8400 GB=8,400,000 MB 8,400,000 MB/400 MB/s=21,000 s≈5.8 hours8,400,000 \text{ MB} / 400 \text{ MB/s} = 21,000 \text{ s} \approx 5.8 \text{ hours}8,400,000 MB/400 MB/s=21,000 s≈5.8 hours

In production, the move is throttled to avoid impacting customer traffic. Throttle to 200 MB/s aggregate (50% of theoretical): 11.7 hours. Throttle further during business hours and run faster overnight: actual wall-clock could be 15-24 hours.

Anya schedules the move starting at 8 PM on a weekday. By morning, ~70% complete; the remainder finishes during the next day at reduced rate. By 36 hours after start, the cluster is rebalanced.

Costs:

* Network throughput: 200 MB/s sustained for 24 hours = 17 TB transferred (egress fees may apply if cross-AZ).
* Cluster CPU: ~10-20% extra per node during the move (LSM compaction overhead, Raft snapshot streaming).
* Customer-visible: p99 latency may increase by 10-30%, which Anya monitors and throttles if it exceeds SLA.

**Q2.** A team is implementing a multi-tenant SaaS database. Each tenant has its own set of rows. They are choosing between (a) hash partitioning by tenant ID, (b) range partitioning by (tenant ID, row ID), (c) one database per tenant. Analyze trade-offs.

Hint

Hash by tenant: each tenant's data is on one partition; cross-tenant queries are easy. Range by (tenant, row): tenant data is locally sorted. One DB per tenant: max isolation, high operational cost.

**Answer:**

(a) **Hash partitioning by tenant ID.** Each tenant's data is on one partition (potentially one node). Pros: per-tenant queries are single-partition; tenant data has locality; resharding moves tenant data atomically. Cons: a large tenant can grow to dominate one partition (hot tenant problem); the system cannot split one tenant's data across nodes; cross-tenant analytical queries scatter.

(b) **Range partitioning by (tenant ID, row ID).** Tenants are sorted; within each tenant, rows are sorted. Pros: large tenants' data can span multiple ranges (split when too large); per-tenant range scans are efficient; small tenants are co-located on the same range. Cons: small-tenant adjacency means a hot small tenant can affect its neighbors; range metadata is more complex.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
(c) **One database per tenant.** Each tenant has its own database (or schema, namespace, project). Pros: maximum isolation; per-tenant resource control; per-tenant deletion is trivial. Cons: operational cost scales with tenant count (managing thousands of databases); cross-tenant aggregations are very hard; per-tenant overhead (connection pools, schema versions).

Recommended:

* For 10s to 100s of tenants: option (c) (database-per-tenant) is operationally manageable and gives the best isolation.
* For 1000s of tenants: option (b) (range partitioning) handles the long-tail tenant distribution best (small tenants co-located, large tenants split as needed).
* For 100,000+ tenants: option (a) (hash by tenant) provides the simplest sharding but requires application-level work to handle hot tenants.

The Salesforce / Workday pattern (massive multi-tenancy) is usually option (b) plus careful schema design. The startup SaaS pattern (a few hundred tenants) is often option (c) for simplicity.

**Q3.** A team is choosing between RocksDB (LSM) and SQLite (B+ tree) as the embedded storage for a key-value store. Workload: 80% writes, 20% reads, random access pattern, 100 GB total dataset on SSD. Compare and recommend.

Hint

Heavy writes favor LSM. SSD reduces but does not eliminate the B+ tree random-write disadvantage.

**Answer:** Workload characteristics:

* 80% writes, 20% reads: write-heavy.
* Random access: no sequential locality benefit for either system.
* 100 GB on SSD: large but not enormous; SSD reduces random-I/O cost.

RocksDB profile:

* Write throughput: very high (memtable + WAL sequential). For 80% write workload, RocksDB handles it well.
* Read latency: each read may touch the memtable + Bloom filters + multiple SSTables. p99 for cold reads can be 1-5 ms.
* Space amplification: 1.5-2x typical (multiple SSTables before compaction).
* Compaction overhead: periodic background CPU and I/O bursts.

SQLite profile:

* Write throughput: moderate. Each write must update a B+ tree page; random updates cost page-level I/O.
* Read latency: very low (single page read per point lookup).
* Space amplification: ~1x (in-place updates).
* Operational simplicity: SQLite is the easiest embedded database to operate.

Recommendation: RocksDB for this workload. The 80% write ratio means RocksDB's write-throughput advantage dominates; even on SSD, B+ tree's random writes are 5-10x slower than LSM's sequential writes for sustained high throughput. The 20% read ratio still works well in RocksDB with Bloom filters for point lookups.

Exception: if the team values operational simplicity over peak performance, SQLite may still be the right call. SQLite's "it just works" property is a real advantage; RocksDB requires tuning (compaction strategy, write-buffer size, block cache size) that a small team may not want to invest in. For a 100 GB dataset that grows slowly, SQLite's slower write path may be tolerable.

blocks.en_title: Chapter 12: Sharding, Partitioning, Resharding, and LSM-Tree Foundations
blocks.src:
#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Defend or refute: "In 2026, all distributed databases should use range partitioning with auto-split. Hash partitioning is for systems that haven't matured."

**Discussion:** Defense: range partitioning with auto-split (CockroachDB, Spanner) handles hot-key issues that hash partitioning cannot. The system can detect a hot range and split it; a hot key in a hash-partitioned system stays on one node until application change. This is operational maturity.

Refutation: hash partitioning is genuinely simpler. For workloads with uniform key distribution (no skew), hash gives more predictable performance with less metadata overhead. Cassandra and DynamoDB are not less mature than CockroachDB; they have different design priorities (massive horizontal scale-out, predictable per-node performance).

The synthesis: range with auto-split is the right default for workloads with unpredictable skew (most OLTP). Hash is the right default for workloads where the application controls key distribution (cache, session store). Modern systems offer both per-table; the choice is not "which system" but "which scheme per table."

A second consideration: range partitioning's metadata overhead is real. For a system with millions of small ranges (CockroachDB at large scale), the metadata layer becomes a significant operational concern. Hash partitioning sidesteps this; the trade-off is the lost flexibility.

**Q2.** An LLM is asked to "implement consistent hashing for our distributed cache" and produces 50 lines of code. Identify three structural concerns with the LLM-generated code that distinguish it from a production implementation.

**Discussion:**

(a) **Vnode handling.** Production consistent hashing uses virtual nodes (256+ per physical node) for load distribution. LLM-generated code typically uses one position per node, leading to load imbalance.

(b) **Token assignment**. Production systems carefully assign tokens to ensure no replica of a key lands on the same physical node. LLM code may not handle the multi-replica case correctly, allowing two replicas of the same key to land on the same node.

(c) **Routing under membership change.** Production code handles concurrent reads/writes during a node addition or removal correctly: writes go to the new owner, reads check both old and new owners until the migration completes. LLM code typically treats membership change as instantaneous, which is wrong under concurrent traffic.

Three more (any of which is a production bug):

(d) **Hash function choice.** Production uses cryptographic-quality hash (MurmurHash3, FNV) for load distribution. LLM code may use `hash()` (which is not designed for uniformity).

(e) **Edge cases in vnode count.** When physical nodes have different capacities (heterogeneous cluster), vnode counts should be proportional. LLM code typically assumes uniform vnode counts.
